items.title: volume.fsck -findMissingChunksInFiler -reallyDeleteFilerEntries is slow and CPU-intensive when deleting a large number of filer entries
items.body:
When using volume.fsck with the flags -findMissingChunksInFiler and -reallyDeleteFilerEntries to clean up orphaned filer entries (i.e., filer metadata referencing missing volume chunks), the operation is significantly slow and consumes high CPU resources when dealing with a large number of entries.

In our test environment, deleting 1,000,000 image file entries took approximately 5 minutes and consistently consumed ~15% CPU on an Intel i5-12400 processor throughout the entire process.

This performance characteristic makes the command impractical for routine maintenance on large-scale deployments, as the operation window becomes unacceptably long and the sustained CPU load may impact other services running on the same node.

items.title: redis2: harden the orphaned index member cleanup
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

Follow-ups to #10735's `removeOrphanedDirectoryListMember`, from reviewing it in depth. Stacked on that PR — the first two commits here are its commits; review the last five.

Four gaps in the compensation, each its own commit:

1. **The helper's parameters were mutually derivable.** `dirListKey` arrived pre-prefixed while `path` arrived raw and was prefixed inside — a mix-up at a future call site (double prefix, missing prefix) would silently `ZREM` the wrong member. The helper now takes `(ctx, dirPath, fileName)` and derives both keys itself.

2. **Super large directories.** The PR argued the cleanup is unreachable for them because the index key never exists — not true for a directory converted to super large after accumulating members: the legacy ZSET lingers, listings still return its members, and the cleanup would strip them irrecoverably (recreates never re-add, since `InsertEntry` skips the `ZAdd`). The helper now carries the same `isSuperLargeDirectory` guard as `InsertEntry`, `DeleteEntry` and `DeleteFolderChildren`.

3. **The repair was not failure-atomic.** The `ZREM` and the restoring `ZAddNX` ran on the listing request's context, so a client disconnect mid-repair canceled the restore after the removal had landed — permanently de-indexing a live, concurrently recreated entry — and the failed restore was discarded without a log line. The repair now runs on `context.WithoutCancel` and a failed restore is logged.

4. **Directory orphans.** For a member whose value key was lost (eviction, out-of-band `DEL`) but whose own child index still exists, stripping the member detaches a live subtree: nothing can list it or recursively delete it afterwards, and its keys leak forever. Empty ZSETs self-delete, so a present index means children — such a member is now kept, matching the pre-#10735 behavior where the lingering member kept the subtree reachable to `DeleteFolderChildren`.

# How is the PR tested?

Two new gated tests (super large guard, directory with live children), and the recreated-entry test now runs under both key prefixes like the orphan test — with a single-prefix test, a dropped or doubled prefix on the `EXISTS` key passes the whole suite. Harness: the client is closed even when the `PING` fails, and the dead `loadSuperLargeDirectories(nil)` ritual is gone. Full suite passes with `-race` against a live Redis.

items.title: redis: remove orphaned directory index members on listing
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

The `redis` (v1) store has the same defect #10735 fixes in `redis2`: the listing's not-found branch logs and continues without removing the directory-index member, so a member whose value key is gone — TTL expiry, eviction, an out-of-band `DEL` — stays in the parent's SET forever. v1 is worse off than redis2 here, because `ListDirectoryEntries` loads the whole member set with no pagination, so every dead member inflates every single listing of that directory.

# How are we solving the problem?

Same shape as the redis2 fix, with the sharp edges found in its review already filed off:

- `SRem` the member, re-check the value key, and `SAdd` it back when the value is present again — a concurrent recreate's `SAdd` can land before our `SRem`, and this is what keeps that entry listed. Converges in both interleavings for the same reason as in #10735: `InsertEntry` writes the value before the member.
- A member whose value is gone but whose own child index still exists is kept, not stripped: empty sets self-delete in Redis, so a present index means live children, and detaching it would leave the subtree unreachable to a later recursive delete.
- The repair runs on `context.WithoutCancel` so a client disconnect mid-listing cannot tear it half-done, and a failed restore is logged instead of discarded.

Single-key commands only, so behavior is identical on all `UniversalClient` transports.

# How is the PR tested?

`weed/filer/redis/universal_redis_store_test.go`, gated on `RUN_REDIS_TESTS=1` like the redis2 suite (`REDIS_ADDR` defaults to `127.0.0.1:6379`): orphan removal through the listing, a recreated entry surviving the repair, and a directory with live children keeping its member. All pass with `-race` against redis-server 8 (docker `redis:7` as well); the orphan test fails on master.

items.title: filer: free orphaned hard-link chunks and remote objects in delete sweeps
items.body: ## Summary Follow-ups to #11785 (which fixed the core of #11754 — a replayed directory delete now sweeps the lagging peer's subtree and queues its chunks). These commits close the gaps the sweep left around entries that don't own their data the usual way: - **`filer: free shared chunks when a folder delete drops the last hard link`** — `doBatchDeleteFolderMetaAndData` skipped chunk collection for every hard-linked child. When the recursive delete removed the inode's last link, the shared record was deleted and nobody was left to free the chunks. The child path now checks whether the record survived (`hardLinkIsOrphaned`) and queues the entry's chunks when it did not. - **`filer: free orphaned hard-link chunks in the replayed delete sweep`** — same leak on the replication path: the sweep skipped all hard-linked children unconditionally. After the store delete drops the inode record, the child's chunks are queued like any other swept entry. - **`filer: mirror remote-object cleanup in the replayed delete sweep`** — children a lagging peer alone still held were dropped with plain store deletes: their remote objects leaked, and lazy remote fetches could resurrect them. The sweep now records event-timestamped remote-deletion tombstones and calls `maybeDeleteFromRemoteIfUnchanged` for non-directory children (mirroring `doBatchDeleteFolderMetaAndData`). Metadata-only deletes (`Seaweed-X-Keep-Remote-Object`) and cross-cluster events keep the origin's semantics. - **`filerstore: return real errors from KvGet on MongoDB, ArangoDB, Elastic`** — these stores mapped every lookup failure to `ErrKvNotFound`, so a database error looked identical to a missing key: `hardLinkIsOrphaned` could treat a live inode record as gone and free chunks other links still own. `ErrKvNotFound` now means genuinely absent. - **`filer: bind remote-object deletes to the observed object version`** — a guarded stat-then-delete still let a replacement landing between the two requests go down with the deleted object. New optional `remote_storage.RemoteStorageConditionalDeleter` deletes only while the object is still the one a stat described — S3 `If-Match`, GCS `GenerationMatch`, Azure `IfMatch` — used by the replay sweep and the write-back daemon's delete/rename-source paths. Backends without it keep the guarded stat-then-delete. Notes for the enterprise merge: `weed/filer` in seaweedfs.com still carries the pre-#11785 `Replay`, so the sweep port needs the sealed-dir handling (`SegmentChunks`, `ErrDirectorySealed`) and `CacheChunks` on top — enterprise `GetChunks()` does not include `CacheChunks`, so the hardlink hunk should append both. Go and Rust volume servers are unaffected: the filer emits fileId deletions through the same `BatchDelete` surface either way. #### Test plan - [x] Issue #11754 reproduction (2 filers, SIGSTOP lag, `N=2000`): `0/2000` orphans on both filers, `2000/2000` needles freed - [x] `go test ./weed/filer/` — including new tests for last/surviving hard links on both paths, remote sweep/tombstone/metadata-only behavior, and conditional-delete use - [ ] CI --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Remote files are deleted only when they still match the version recorded by SeaweedFS, helping prevent newer or replaced files from being removed during synchronization and cleanup. * Metadata updates keep the local record aligned with the remote file’s latest version when that information is available. * Recursive folder deletion preserves chunks referenced by hard-linked files and removes orphaned chunks when the last link is deleted. * Storage lookup failures are reported as errors instead of being mistaken for missing records. * Directory cleanup handles child-lock conflicts with retries and preserves newer or otherwise changed entries.

items.title: fix(redis2): remove orphaned directory index members on listing
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

The `redis2` per-directory child index — the ZSET at `<dir>\x00` — accumulates members whose value key no longer exists, and nothing ever removes them.

`ListDirectoryEntries` reads the members, then calls `FindEntry` per member (`weed/filer/redis2/universal_redis_store.go:189-231`). Two outcomes matter:

- the value key is gone → `filer_pb.ErrNotFound` → the loop logs and `continue`s, **leaving the member in the index** (`:205-211` before this change);
- the value key is there but the entry is logically expired (`Crtime + TtlSec < now`) → `DEL` the value **and `ZREM` the member** (`:213-219`).

The second branch is the intended behaviour — the code already means to keep the index consistent. The first branch is the one that actually runs for TTL entries, because the two expiry deadlines are on different clocks:

- `doInsertEntry` writes `SET <key> <value> EX <TtlSec>` (`:86`), so Redis drops the key at `set_time + TtlSec`;
- the filer's logical check is `Crtime + TtlSec < now`.

`Crtime` is stamped before the store write, so `Crtime <= set_time` and the logical deadline is the *earlier* of the two — by the sub-millisecond gap between stamping the attribute and Redis processing the `SET`. The `else` branch can therefore only run if a listing lands inside that gap. Every listing after it finds `GET` returning `redis.Nil` and takes the not-found branch, the one that leaves the member behind. (An entry that is later *updated* re-arms the Redis TTL from the update time while `Crtime` stays put, which is the only case where the working branch is reliably reachable — so the leak is specific to entries created once and never touched again, which is the common TTL case.)

Under a TTL workload the index therefore grows without bound, and two things get worse with it:

- `LIST` costs one `GET` round trip per name *ever created* in that directory, not per live entry;
- the skip logs at `glog.V(0)`, which is on by default, so every listing emits one log line per dead member.

The same orphan is produced by any other route that removes a value key without the matching `ZREM` — an out-of-band `DEL`, `maxmemory` eviction, or a `DeleteEntry` that fails between its `DEL` and its `ZREM` (`:119-143`). TTL is just the one that does it continuously.

# How are we solving the problem?

`ZREM` the member in the not-found branch, mirroring what the expiry branch already does below and against the same `dirListKey` variable — guarded against a concurrent recreate, per the review point below.

Things I checked rather than assumed:

**A member cannot legitimately outlive a missing value.** `InsertEntry` writes the value first and adds the member second (`:56-74`): `doInsertEntry`'s `SET` has returned before `ZAddNX` is issued. So "member present" implies "value was written at some point", and a member returned by `ZRangeByLex` whose value is absent has had that value deleted or expired — it is never an entry mid-creation. The opposite window (value written, member not yet added) does exist, but a listing cannot observe it, because it only iterates members.

**The value can, however, come back before the `ZREM` lands** — which the paragraph above does not cover, and which both review bots caught. If an `InsertEntry` for the same path completes between `FindEntry` returning `ErrNotFound` and the `ZREM`, its `ZAddNX` is a no-op, because the member is still in place; the `ZREM` then strips the index member off a live value. `UpdateEntry` only calls `doInsertEntry` (`:92-95`) and never re-adds the member, so the entry stays invisible to `ListDirectoryEntries` and `DeleteFolderChildren` until another `InsertEntry` hits that exact path. That is a real regression, so the cleanup compensates rather than removing unconditionally: `ZREM`, re-check the value key, and `ZAddNX` the member back when the value is present again or when the check itself failed.

That converges in both interleavings. If the insert's `SET` lands before the re-check, the re-check sees it and restores the member; if it lands after, the insert's own `ZAddNX` is necessarily after our `ZREM` and restores the member itself. Only a positively confirmed absent value leaves the member removed, so the repair still converges for genuine orphans at the cost of one extra `EXISTS` — on the repair path only, which is one-time per orphan.

The remedy both reviews suggested — a Lua script or `MULTI` spanning the value key and the index key — is not available here. `RedisCluster2Store` embeds `UniversalRedis2Store`, and the two keys (`<prefix></dir/name>` and `<prefix></dir>\x00`) carry no hash tag, so a multi-key script would be `CROSSSLOT` under `redis_cluster2`. The compensating form uses only single-key commands and behaves identically on all three transports.

**`keyPrefix`.** `dirListKey` is `store.getKey(genDirectoryListKey(...))` at `:178` — already prefixed — and the new `ZREM` reuses that variable instead of rebuilding the key. Rebuilding it unprefixed would have been a silent no-op for every deployment that sets `keyPrefix`, which is why the test runs both with and without one.

**Transient errors cannot trigger it.** `FindEntry` returns the bare `filer_pb.ErrNotFound` sentinel only for `redis.Nil` (`:99-102`); every other failure is wrapped with `fmt.Errorf`. The branch guard is `err == filer_pb.ErrNotFound` — identity, not `errors.Is` — so a connection blip cannot match it and still breaks out of the loop as before.

**Super-large directories.** `isSuperLargeDirectory` makes `InsertEntry` skip the `ZAdd` and `DeleteEntry` skip the `ZRem`, so the index key does not exist for those directories at all. `ZRangeByLex` returns nothing, the loop body never runs, and the new call is unreachable. The feature is unaffected.

Cleanup failures still do not fail the listing — a failed repair is simply retried on the next one — but the errors are no longer discarded outright, since the restore decision depends on them: a `ZREM` that errors removes nothing and returns, and a re-check that errors restores the member, so the failure modes bias towards a stale member rather than a lost one.

**Deliberately not included:** making the physical TTL a backstop behind the logical one (`SET ... EX TtlSec + grace`) so the logical branch wins the race and performs the clean two-part delete. That changes when data actually disappears from Redis for every `redis2` user, and it would not remove the need for this fix, since the non-TTL routes above produce the same orphan. Happy to raise it separately if you want it.

**Also deliberately not included:** the expiry branch at `:214-219` has a pre-existing instance of the same race, with a worse outcome — a concurrent `InsertEntry` landing between `FindEntry` and the `DEL` loses the freshly written value, not just the index member. Closing it needs a compare-and-delete on the value rather than the compensating restore used here, so it is a separate change and not one I want to smuggle into this one.

# How is the PR tested?

New `weed/filer/redis2/universal_redis_store_test.go`. It needs a live Redis, so it follows the existing convention for store tests that need a server — `tarantool_store_test.go` gating on `RUN_TARANTOOL_TESTS=1`, `foundationdb_store_test.go` skipping when the cluster is absent — and skips unless `RUN_REDIS_TESTS=1`, with `REDIS_ADDR` defaulting to `127.0.0.1:6379`. Each test works inside a uniquely named directory and cleans up after itself, so it is safe against a shared instance.

I did try the in-tree `tempredis` helper used by `redis3/kv_directory_children_test.go` first. It hangs on any current `redis-server`: it blocks waiting for the literal line `The server is now ready to accept connections`, which Redis stopped printing years ago. That helper is only reachable from a `Benchmark` today, so nothing noticed. Worth knowing if anyone tries to build on it.

- `TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesOrphanedIndexMembers` — two entries, one's value key dropped; asserts the listing returns only the live entry *and* that the index is left holding only the live name. Run with `keyPrefix` empty and set.
- `TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesIndexMembersExpiredByRedis` — inserts with `TtlSec: 1`, waits past it, asserts Redis has already dropped the value key, then asserts the listing empties the index. This is the reported path end to end.
- `TestRemoveOrphanedDirectoryListMemberKeepsRecreatedEntry` — added for the review point above. It drives the cleanup with the value key present, which is exactly the state a concurrent recreate leaves behind, and asserts the member survives and the entry still lists. Asserted at the helper rather than through `ListDirectoryEntries`, because the window between the `GET` and the `ZREM` cannot be hit deterministically from outside. It fails if the restore is removed.

Against `redis-server 8.2.1`, the first three cases fail on master and pass with the change:

```
--- FAIL: TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesOrphanedIndexMembers/keyPrefix=
        directory index holds [alive orphan], want [alive]
--- FAIL: TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesOrphanedIndexMembers/keyPrefix=sw:
        directory index holds [alive orphan], want [alive]
--- FAIL: TestListDirectoryEntriesRemovesIndexMembersExpiredByRedis
        directory index holds [ttl], want none
```

`go build ./weed/...`, `go vet ./weed/filer/redis2/`, `gofmt` all clean, and `go test ./weed/filer/redis2/... -race` passes against a live Redis.

## Note on `redis3`, which I am not touching

`redis3` has the same shape at `universal_redis_store.go:140-166`, and is worse off: its not-found branch removes nothing at all, and its expiry branch calls `ZRem` on `<dir>\x00` — which in `redis3` is a **string** holding the serialised skiplist root (`kv_directory_children.go:43`), not a ZSET. That returns `WRONGTYPE`, the result is discarded, and it has therefore never removed anything.

Flagging rather than fixing, because `weed/filer/redis3/README.md` reads `Desuppported.` and the store has no section in `weed/command/scaffold/filer.toml`, so any fix there would be to a store nobody is being pointed at. Say the word if you would like it repaired anyway.

## Related

#10736 proposes giving lazily-created remote-mount entries a TTL so the filer's existing expiry machinery reclaims them. The two compose: that change makes TTL entries the normal case for a whole class of deployment, and this one is what stops the directory index growing anyway when they expire.

- [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.
- [x] All AI code review comments have been addressed. No more comments to fix if reviewed again. Reviewer may request additional gemini and copilot reviews.

items.title: redis2: orphan cleanup existence checks must not read replicas
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

Under `redis_cluster2` with `useReadOnly` or `routeByLatency`, go-redis routes read-flagged commands (`GET`, `EXISTS`) to replicas while writes go to the master. That turns the #10735 cleanup destructive under replica lag: an insert lands on the master, a listing's `GET` hits a replica that has not applied it yet, the not-found branch fires, the `ZREM` removes the live member on the master — and the compensating `EXISTS` asks the same lagging replica, gets 0, and skips the restore. The entry vanishes from every listing until it is re-inserted. Before the cleanup existed, that same stale read cost a transient one-page miss, not a lost index member.

Stacked on #10744; review the last two commits.

# How are we solving the problem?

The repair's two existence checks now run as a single-key `EVAL` (`return redis.call('EXISTS', KEYS[1])`). Scripts may write, so every transport routes them to the key slot's master — the check can no longer be answered from a stale view, and the cleanup stays enabled for replica-read deployments instead of being config-gated off. Single key, so no `CROSSSLOT` concern, and on non-cluster transports it is the same node it always was. Where `EVAL` is unavailable the check errors and the repair keeps the member — the fail-safe direction it already had.

The triggering `GET` itself may still read a lagging replica, but that now converges: the `ZREM` lands on the master, the master-side check sees the value, and the member is restored.

Second commit: the scaffold documented this store's read-routing key as `readOnly`, but the code reads `useReadOnly` — anyone enabling it through the documented key got master-only routing silently.

# How is the PR tested?

The existing gated suite exercises the script path in every repair test and passes with `-race` against a live Redis. Replica lag itself is not reproducible on a single node; the argument above is the go-redis routing rule (scripts never take the replica path).

items.title: redis2: expire entries without destroying a concurrent recreate
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

The pre-existing race #10735 deliberately left open, with a worse outcome than the one it fixed: the logical-expiry branch in `ListDirectoryEntries` does an unconditional `DEL` of the value plus a bare `ZREM` of the member. A concurrent `InsertEntry` landing between the lister's `GET` and that `DEL` loses the freshly written value — not just an index member, the data. Its `ZAddNX` no-ops against the still-present member, so the recreate leaves neither value nor listing.

Stacked on #10743; review the last commit.

# How are we solving the problem?

The multi-key `MULTI`/Lua form is still off the table (`CROSSSLOT` under `redis_cluster2`, the value and index keys carry no hash tag), but the value delete only needs to be atomic against the value key itself, and single-key scripts are cluster-safe. The expiry branch now:

- re-reads the value and re-checks logical expiry on those exact bytes — a recreate that already landed is simply kept;
- deletes through a single-key compare-and-delete script, so the `DEL` fires only if the value still holds the bytes the decision was made on — a recreate that lands mid-flight survives untouched;
- removes the member through `removeOrphanedDirectoryListMember` instead of a bare `ZREM`, which restores the member if an insert races the removal, and reuses the not-found repair when the redis TTL won the race after all.

The expiry predicate moves into `isLogicallyExpired` so the loop and the recheck cannot drift apart. Costs one extra `GET` per expired entry, on the expiry path only.

# How is the PR tested?

Three new gated tests: end-to-end listing of a logically expired entry (value and member both gone, under both key prefixes — deterministic, no sleeps: `Crtime` an hour back with a 60s TTL keeps the physical key alive while logically expired), a recreate racing the expiry decision (value and member both survive), and the compare-and-delete script refusing mismatched bytes. Full suite passes with `-race` against a live Redis.

items.body: ## Summary - When replica fan-out rolls back copies that already landed, the `type=replicate` DELETE reuses the assignment's write JWT. An unresponsive holder holds the upload open past that token's 10 s expiry, so the surviving holders answer 401 and keep the orphaned needle. - `deleteChunkFromHolders` now retries once with a fresh token minted through a new optional `LookupJwtFunc` hook on `ChunkedUploadOption` when a holder rejects the delete as unauthorized. - Callers that can reach the master supply the hook: the s3api keeps its master client on the server and mints via `operation.LookupJwt`, and the admin file browser does the same through its master client. Callers without master access keep the previous best-effort behaviour. - Regression test: a fake holder that 401s the stale token and accepts the renewed one. #### Test plan - [x] `go test ./weed/operation/` — package green, incl. new `TestDeleteChunkFromHoldersRenewsExpiredJwt` - [x] `go vet ./weed/operation/ ./weed/s3api/ ./weed/admin/handlers/` - [x] `go build` on all touched packages Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Failed chunked uploads can now retry cleanup when a holder rejects a deletion request as unauthorized. A fresh authorization token is obtained, and deletion is retried once for that holder, helping prevent uploaded chunks from being left behind. * Authorization lookups now honor request cancellation and deadlines, stopping when the associated operation is canceled or times out.

items.title: volume.fsck: run all filer-entry purges through the shared worker pool
items.body: ## What this fixes #11924 added the `-purgeConcurrency` worker pool for `-findMissingChunksInFiler -reallyDeleteFilerEntries`, but only wired it into the missing-*volume* branch of `collectFilerFileIdAndPaths`. The per-volume check in `oneVolumeFileIdsCheckOneVolume` — the path that deletes the bulk of orphan entries (filer metadata pointing at needles absent from a volume that still exists) — still issues one synchronous HTTP DELETE per orphan inside the file-read loop. ## Changes - `volume.fsck` now starts the shared purge pool once for the whole `-findMissingChunksInFiler` run and threads the queue through `findFilerChunksMissingInVolumeServers` → `oneVolumeFileIdsCheckOneVolume`; the pool is drained before the empty-directory sweep. - The filer fid file now persists each entry's `hardLinkId`, and `readFilerFileIdFile` returns it, so orphans queued by the per-volume check hash into the pool by hard link id exactly like the missing-volume path — two paths sharing an id still serialize on one worker and can't race the shared hard-link counter. - Test: `TestVolumeFsckCheckOneVolumeQueuesOrphansWithHardLinkId` seeds a volume idx + fid file and asserts the two orphans are queued with their hard link ids. Addresses #11009 (follow-up to #11924). --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Volume filesystem checks now queue orphaned filer entries for cleanup while preserving their hard-link relationships. * Cleanup workers finish after checks, including when empty directories are purged or the check encounters an error. * Invalid or truncated hard-link information is now reported rather than silently ignored. * Metadata saves now complete worker cleanup when generating the starting path entry fails.

items.title: filer: sweep the local subtree on a replayed directory delete
items.body: ## Summary - A recursive `DELETE /dir?recursive=true` emits one event for the directory key only, so peers applied it with a single `DeleteEntry`. Children the peer held that the deleting filer had not yet replayed stayed orphaned — unlisted but still readable by path — and their chunks were never deleted. - On replaying a directory delete, the peer now sweeps its local subtree (recursively collecting chunk ids when the origin deleted chunk data) before dropping the directory key, so orphans are removed and their needles freed. #### Test plan - [x] `go test ./weed/filer/` — new coverage asserts a replayed directory delete removes nested children, and that file deletes keep siblings Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Directory deletions processed during metadata replay now remove older local descendants, preventing deleted content from reappearing. * Newer descendants and the ancestor directories needed to retain them are preserved, and retained directories prevent stale child entries from returning. * File deletions leave sibling entries intact. * When chunk deletion is requested, chunks associated with removed files in the deleted subtree are queued for deletion.

items.title: iceberg maintenance: match percent-decoded keys when checking file references
items.body: ## Summary Fixes #11976 — after a maintenance run overlapped a writer commit, tables lost live data files and subsequent reads returned `NoSuchKey`. **Root cause:** writers can percent-escape partition directory names in the `file_path` they record in manifests (the reported table kept data under `data/month_collected_at_1%3D681/`). The S3 layer decodes the object key before the entry lands on the filer, so the object actually lives at `data/month_collected_at_1=681/`. `remove_orphans` compared the escaped reference path against the decoded filer path, counted the live file as an orphan, and deleted it once it passed the age window. The maintenance job's commits also explain the 409 `branch "main" has changed` the reporter saw — the same run both moved `main` and swept the files. Changes: - `remove_orphans`: the referenced-path set now includes the percent-decoded spelling of every reference, so escaped references still cover the objects the S3 layer stored. - `expire_snapshots`: the kept-file set gets the same dual-spelling coverage, and expired files are deleted at their decoded key — the location the S3 layer actually wrote. - `lookupFileByIcebergPath`: when a lookup misses and the reference contains escapes, retry once at the decoded spelling so compaction/expiry can read files recorded under escaped paths instead of erroring out. #### Test plan - [x] `TestRemoveOrphansKeepsPercentEscapedReferences` — fails before the fix (live file swept), passes after - [x] `TestLookupFileByIcebergPathDecodesEscapedReference` — escaped ref resolves to decoded key; a file genuinely stored at an escaped name still resolves verbatim - [x] `go test ./weed/worker/tasks/iceberg/` — full package green Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Iceberg file lookups now handle percent-escaped paths, including decoded paths and filenames containing literal escape sequences. * Snapshot expiration and orphan cleanup recognize escaped and decoded paths consistently, preserving files referenced by snapshots and identifying unrelated orphaned files. * Missing files during snapshot expiration no longer generate warnings, and files resolved outside the table path are protected from deletion. * Lookups retry decoded path spellings when the original path is not found; other lookup errors are returned without retry. * Shell startup retries filer discovery when no filer address is configured, until one is found or the discovery timeout expires.

items.title: filer: persist pending chunk deletions across restarts (durable deletion ledger)
items.body: ## Problem A filer's pending file deletions live in a RAM-only `UnboundedQueue`. If a filer crashes or restarts while deletions are queued, those pending chunk deletions are **lost forever** — the chunks stay on volume servers as permanent orphans. In multi-filer setups with restart flaps this is a major, silent source of orphaned data. The TODO in `weed/filer/filer_deletion.go` proposed consuming the inbound queue into the outbound one on shutdown, but that does **not** fix it: an outbound `Consume()` whose retry later fails leaves the fileId in neither queue. ## What this PR does Make pending deletions **durable** with a small KV-backed ledger (`weed/filer/filer_deletion_persist.go`): - Every queued deletion is recorded in a dedicated filer-store KV entry (`/.sys/deletion_ledger`), keyed by filer host:port so the 3 filers of a deployment don't collide. - On filer start (`SetStore`), the ledger is replayed: pending deletions re-enter the retry queue, so a crash never loses the intent to delete. - Items are forgotten from the ledger **only on terminal outcomes** (success / not-found / permanent error); retryable failures keep them tracked. - Periodic snapshots + a final snapshot on `Shutdown()` bound the replay-on-restart window to the last snapshot interval. - On startup, `reloadDeletionLedger()` re-queues recovered ids after a grace window so the initial peer meta-aggregation settles first. This avoids a new hazard: purging a chunk that a lagging peer is about to re-reference as live data (stale replay otherwise turns a stale read into a dangling read). - Volume deletes are idempotent (not-found == success), so re-deleting after a crash never double-frees. - Kill switch via viper: `filer.deleteQueue.persist=false` opts out entirely (reload also refuses to recover so a stale ledger never comes back). Tunables: `filer.deleteQueue.persistInterval`, `.recoveryGrace`. ## Testing `go test -race ./weed/filer/` green, including: - `TestDeletionLedgerPersistsAcrossRestart` — queue deletions, "restart" (new Filer + SetStore), assert the pending deletions come back and converge. - `TestDeletionLedgerForgetsTerminalOutcomes` — success and not-found paths clear the ledger; retryable outcomes keep entries. - Disabled-switch and zero-value `Filer` safety cases. Build: `go build ./...` green. gofmt clean. ## Related Independent of the meta-log-collection branch (`fix/meta-log-collection`) — no functional overlap, either can merge first. Together they cut the two sources of post-flap junk in the `default` collection: - this PR stops orphaned **user chunks** leaking when a filer crash loses its RAM-only deletion queue - `fix/meta-log-collection` stops the internal **metadata log** from living in the default collection in the first place --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Reliability** * Pending file deletions are saved and recovered after a restart, helping cleanup continue if the filer shuts down before deletions finish. * Deletions that can be retried remain tracked until they succeed or are resolved, reducing the risk of files being left behind. * Deletion records are kept separate for each filer, and recovered deletions resume after a brief recovery period. * Deletion records are saved during normal operation and when the filer shuts down.

items.title: filer: recursive delete through one filer leaves a lagging peer's children behind as unlisted entries; their chunks are never freed (204 returned)
items.body:
### Summary

With two or more filers replicating each other (Filer Store Replication), a recursive `DELETE /dir?recursive=true` sent to one filer only removes the children **that filer has already seen**. The peers apply the replicated directory delete with `Replay`, which deletes **only the directory's own key**. Any children a peer holds that the deleting filer had not replayed yet stay in the peer's store:

- they are no longer listed (the parent entry is gone), but are still readable by exact path;
- their chunks are never deleted, so the needles leak permanently (nothing references them through a listable path, and `volume.vacuum` keeps them);
- the client gets `204 No Content`, so nothing signals a partial delete.

The reverse also happens: create events the deleting filer replays *after* its delete are inserted under a parent that no longer exists, so the deleting filer ends up with orphaned children too.

A peer only needs to be behind for this, e.g. after a restart, a network partition or under load. In production we have 3 filers on LevelDB3. A peer that diverged long ago (it joined before `TraverseBfsMetadata` bootstrap existed) turned this into terabytes of orphaned entries and leaked needles. Recursive project deletes returned 204 in a few milliseconds and freed nothing. Recreating the parent directory makes the "deleted" children reappear.

### Environment

- SeaweedFS **4.48** (`530be3e37337`), plain `weed master` / `weed volume` / 2 × `weed filer`, default store (LevelDB2 via `-defaultStoreDir`), default filer group.
- Same code path on `master` at `590a75b9d699` (see "Code" below).
- Production where we hit it: 4.38 → 4.47, 3 filers, LevelDB3, `-filerGroup`.

### Control: a single filer is fine

On one filer (`weed server -filer`), `DELETE /d?recursive=true` on directories with 50 / 200 / 1000 / 3000 children (one subdirectory and file each) removed every child and freed every needle. The problem needs a second filer.

### Steps to reproduce

Self-contained; needs `weed`, `curl`, `python3`; uses ports 9433, 8180, 8988, 8989. Filer A's lag is simulated with `SIGSTOP`/`SIGCONT`, which is what a slow or briefly partitioned peer looks like to the others.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# a recursive delete through one filer leaves the children that a lagging
# peer filer holds as orphaned (unlisted) entries whose chunks are never freed
set -u
W=${W:-$(mktemp -d)}; N=${N:-2000}
M=127.0.0.1:9433; V=127.0.0.1:8180; A=127.0.0.1:8988; B=127.0.0.1:8989
mkdir -p $W/m $W/v $W/fa $W/fb
weed master -mdir=$W/m -ip=127.0.0.1 -port=9433 -volumeSizeLimitMB=100 >$W/m.log 2>&1 &
weed volume -dir=$W/v -max=20 -mserver=$M -ip=127.0.0.1 -port=8180 >$W/v.log 2>&1 &
sleep 3
weed filer -master=$M -ip=127.0.0.1 -port=8988 -defaultStoreDir=$W/fa >$W/fa.log 2>&1 & PIDA=$!
trap 'kill -CONT $PIDA 2>/dev/null; kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null' EXIT
until curl -s -o /dev/null http://$A/; do sleep 1; done   # start B only once A serves
weed filer -master=$M -ip=127.0.0.1 -port=8989 -defaultStoreDir=$W/fb >$W/fb.log 2>&1 &
until curl -s -o /dev/null http://$B/; do sleep 1; done
until grep -q "loopSubscribeToOneFiler read 127.0.0.1:8989" $W/fa.log && grep -q "aggregate from peers.*8988" $W/fb.log; do sleep 1; done
sleep 3

deletes() { curl -s "http://$V/status" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(sum(v.get("DeleteCount",0) for v in json.load(sys.stdin)["Volumes"]))'; }
listed() { curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' "http://$1/d/?limit=100000" | python3 -c 'import json,sys
try: print(len(json.load(sys.stdin).get("Entries") or []))
except Exception: print("404")'; }
readable() { seq 1 $N | xargs -P 16 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://$1/d/f{}.txt" | grep -c '^200$'; }

# 1. an empty directory /d on both filers
curl -s -o /dev/null -F "file=@-;filename=s" "http://$A/d/seed" <<<seed
curl -s -o /dev/null -X DELETE "http://$A/d/seed"; sleep 2

# 2. filer A lags behind its peer (simulated with SIGSTOP); N files are written into /d through B
kill -STOP $PIDA
seq 1 $N | xargs -P 16 -I{} bash -c "curl -s -o /dev/null -F 'file=@-;filename=f' 'http://$B/d/f{}.txt' <<<'payload {}'"
sleep 2
echo "before: B lists $(listed $B) entries in /d"

# 3. A catches up while a recursive delete of /d arrives through A
d0=$(deletes); kill -CONT $PIDA
echo "DELETE /d?recursive=true via A -> HTTP $(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X DELETE "http://$A/d?recursive=true")"
sleep 10

# 4. result
for f in A B; do eval h=\$$f; echo "filer $f: GET /d/ -> $(listed $h) | children still readable by full path: $(readable $h)/$N"; done
echo "needles deleted on the volume server: $(( $(deletes) - d0 ))/$N"
```

### Observed (two runs on fresh clusters, 4.48)

```
before: B lists 2000 entries in /d
DELETE /d?recursive=true via A -> HTTP 204
filer A: GET /d/ -> 404 | children still readable by full path: 1400/2000
filer B: GET /d/ -> 404 | children still readable by full path: 1416/2000
needles deleted on the volume server: 584/2000
```

```
before: B lists 2000 entries in /d
DELETE /d?recursive=true via A -> HTTP 204
filer A: GET /d/ -> 404 | children still readable by full path: 415/2000
filer B: GET /d/ -> 404 | children still readable by full path: 961/2000
needles deleted on the volume server: 1039/2000
```

The exact numbers depend on how much of B's backlog A replays before the delete runs. With a small N (300), A usually catches up first and nothing leaks.

### Expected

After `DELETE /d?recursive=true` returns 2xx, `/d` and everything below it are gone on every filer, and all 2000 needles are deleted. Or, if the filer cannot guarantee that, it does not report success.

### Code

- The deleting filer lists and deletes only its own children: `doBatchDeleteFolderMetaAndData` → `ListDirectoryEntries` (`weed/filer/filer_delete_entry.go:144` in 4.48). It then `DeleteFolderChildren` on its own store and emits one delete event for the directory (`:207`).
- Peers apply that event with `Replay` (`weed/filer/meta_aggregator.go:584`). That is `filerStore.DeleteEntry(oldPath)` for the directory key only (`weed/filer/meta_replay.go:20`): no subtree delete and no chunk deletion for children the origin never listed.
- Replayed creates are inserted without checking that the parent exists (`meta_replay.go:33`), which produces the orphans on the deleting filer.
- On `master` (`590a75b9d699`), after #11698, `Filer.Replay` is the same: `f.Store.DeleteEntry(ctx, oldPath)` (`meta_replay.go:82`) and `f.Store.InsertEntry` (`:97`), now gated per path by commit timestamp, which does not cover the subtree.

### Possible directions (for discussion)

- When replaying the delete of a **directory** entry, delete the local subtree too (as the origin's recursive delete would), including the chunks of children the origin did not know about.
- Do not insert a replayed entry whose parent was deleted after the entry's commit, or delete its chunks instead.

### Impact

Silent, permanent space leak plus "deleted" data that is still readable by path. In a cluster that ran for years with diverged filers, this hid terabytes of entries and needles. We only found them with an offline scan of the stores (keys whose parent hash has no entry).

items.title: admin: cancelled maintenance task files aren't cleaned up, unbounded growth in `-dataDir/tasks`
items.body:
Every scan cycle, the admin cancels all currently pending tasks of each detected type before re-running detection. Cancelling a task only rewrites its file on disk with `status: cancelled` - it's never deleted. Re-detection then creates a fresh task (new file) for the same volume if it still matches. Nothing cleans up cancelled task files, so for any task type that's detected but never executed (e.g. no worker registered for it), `-dataDir/tasks/` gains one permanently-orphaned file per candidate volume every scan cycle, forever. Only an admin restart clears it.

There seems to be a retention helper for this with no callers, and even if it were wired up it only filters completed/failed tasks, not cancelled ones.
https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/blob/0d93dec1454dad80e3b2592068656d9075f158be/weed/admin/maintenance/maintenance_queue.go#L118

### Repro

- `weed admin` 4.47/4.48, worker running with `-jobType=vacuum,volume_balance` only - EC tasks get detected but never claimed.
- File count in `/data/tasks` right after admin restart: 64 (one `pending` `ec_vol_*` per current EC candidate). 24h later: 4,124. Growth is linear, ~3,300-3,700 files/day, matching (candidate count) × (scan cycles/day).
- `kubelet_volume_stats_inodes_used` for the PVC grows at the same linear rate; filled a 65,536-inode PVC in ~3 weeks.
- Restart drops the count ~98% every time - confirms the only active cleanup is the startup wipe, not anything during uptime.

### Environment

SeaweedFS 4.47.0/4.48.0, official Helm chart, k3s + Longhorn.

admin/worker values:
```yaml

admin:
  enabled: true

  data:
    type: persistentVolumeClaim
    size: 1Gi
    storageClass: longhorn

worker:
  enabled: true
  replicas: 2

  jobType: vacuum,volume_balance

  maxDetect: 1
  maxExecute: 1
```

items.title: EC worker: pin jobs to replica-host workers, late-bind local source
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

An EC encode whose volume lives on host A can still be scheduled on host B. The admin executor ranks idle workers only, so the worker pulls the whole `.dat` across the LAN. Detection also names `Sources[0]` / the lowest server id; execute then `SyncAndSelectBestReplica` and can switch the copy source to another rack even when a local replica is already consistent.

# How are we solving the problem?

Admin executor pick ranked idle workers only, so an EC encode whose volume lived on host A could still run on host B and pull the whole `.dat` across the LAN. Detection named `Sources[0]` / the lowest server id; execute then `SyncAndSelectBestReplica` and could switch the copy source to another rack.

This ranks workers whose Hello host matches any replica first (fallback if the local worker is full). After replicas are consistent (equal FileCount), encode late-binds the copy source to a volume server on the same hostname as worker `-address` (any port on that host is local). Diverged FileCount still uses the max replica.

Scheduler pins jobs to the least-loaded replica-host worker until load K (default 5; K=0 spills immediately). A detection batch is parked on per-worker admin queues; ExecutionConcurrency goroutines pop a home-runnable job or steal when that home queue reaches K. A missing home is stolen onto a free worker; orphaned queues wait 30s so a reconnect blink does not dump jobs (zero disables the wait). Jobs whose replica hostname has no registered worker go to a homeless FIFO: no-home workers take leftover first, then steal; home workers keep own-queue, steal, leftover.

# How is the PR tested?

`go test ./weed/admin/plugin/ ./weed/util/ ./weed/worker/tasks/erasure_coding/ -count=1`

New cases: host-key matching / preferred-worker partition; per-worker queues (pin, steal at K, orphan grace, rehome, homeless FIFO order); late-bind source to worker hostname when FileCount ties.

Also ran worker EC encode on a 4-rack cluster with workers co-located on volume hosts: jobs stay on the replica host below K, and encode pulls from the local volume server instead of crossing the LAN.

items.title: fix: volume.fsck -volumeId purges live chunks referenced from outside the volume's bucket
items.body: # What problem are we solving? **`volume.fsck -volumeId ... -reallyDeleteFromVolume` can delete live chunks that the filer still references.** Since #9347, when every volume named by `-volumeId` belongs to one collection and `/` exists, fsck reads the filer only below that bucket directory. That assumes the bucket is the only place that references the collection's volumes. It is not: **a filer started with `-collection=` writes every file under every path into that collection**, and an `fs.configure` rule can bind any path prefix to it. The filer's own metadata log under `/topics/.system/log` is one such file set. Their chunks sit in the selected volumes but their references live outside the bucket, so the narrowed read never sees them. **fsck reports the chunks as orphans and, with `-reallyDeleteFromVolume`, deletes them. The filer entries remain and reading those files fails.** #11794 already closed this hole for `-collection`, which now always reads from the root. **`-volumeId` on its own still narrows the read**, so the same selection reads a different filer scope depending on whether `-collection` is given. Observed on a 3-filer cluster whose filer runs with `-collection=data`: a `volume.fsck -volumeId -forcePurging -reallyDeleteFromVolume` routine **deleted the chunks of about five months of the metadata log** on the passive side of a backup pair, which only the full read would have counted. # How are we solving the problem? Remove the bucket inference for `-volumeId`. The flag keeps selecting which volumes are collected, compared and purged; **the filer is always read from `/`**, as it is with `-collection` and with no filter. `canPurgeDirectory` keeps refusing the root and the bucket directories, which is all it needs now that the read root is fixed. The `-volumeId` help text says the filer is still read from its root. **No new flags, no proto change.** 14 insertions, 95 deletions. # How is the PR tested? - `go test ./weed/shell/ -run Fsck` passes; `TestVolumeFsckCanPurgeDirectory` is reduced to the root scope. - Read-only on a 3-filer cluster with a PostgreSQL store, filer `-collection=data`, 1.6M entries, `volume.fsck -volumeId 63 -v` on a volume of collection `data` with 3 replicas. items.title: admin: stop leaking cancelled maintenance task files in -dataDir/tasks
items.body: Fixes #11595 ## Summary Every scan cycle `ScanWithTaskDetectors` cancels all pending tasks of each detected type via `CancelPendingTasksByType` and then re-detects them. The cancel path **saved** the cancelled task back to disk, and nothing ever deleted those files — so `-dataDir/tasks/` gained one orphaned `.pb` per candidate volume per scan cycle (~3.5k files/day for the reporter). Only the startup wipe cleared them. Changes (one commit each): - **`CancelPendingTasksByType`**: delete the persisted task file instead of saving `status: cancelled`. Cancelled is terminal — `CompleteTask` already deletes files for terminal tasks; this makes cancel behave the same. The cancelled entry stays in memory for the UI until the next purge. - **`MaintenanceManager.CancelTask`** (UI cancel): same fix — it previously touched only memory, leaving the pending `.pb` on disk where a restart would resurrect the cancelled task as pending. - **Retention**: `CleanupOldTasks` (in-memory) and `ConfigPersistence.CleanupCompletedTasks` (disk) now treat cancelled as terminal too, so cancelled files written by older versions are bounded instead of exempt. - **Wire up `cleanupCompletedTasks`**: it had no callers; it is now invoked from `performCleanup` next to `CleanupOldTasks`, so the on-disk retention bound actually runs during uptime. No exported API changes — the enterprise build is unaffected. The admin maintenance queue is Go-only; `seaweed-worker` has no `src/` yet, so there is no Rust counterpart to mirror. #### Test plan - [x] New tests in `weed/admin/dash/maintenance_task_persistence_test.go` fail on master, pass here: - `TestCancelledTaskFilesDoNotAccumulate` — N add+cancel cycles leave 0 `.pb` files (before: N) - `TestManuallyCancelledTaskFileIsRemoved` — `CancelTask` removes the pending file - `TestCleanupCompletedTasksBoundsCancelledFiles` — cancelled files count toward `MaxCompletedTasks` retention - [x] `go test ./weed/admin/...` — all pass - [x] `go vet` clean --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Cancelling a task that is no longer pending now returns an error. * Cancelled task files are removed from persisted task state, preventing files from accumulating. * Retention cleanup now includes cancelled tasks and removes older cancelled task history, keeping stored task history within the configured limit. * Stale task-state snapshots can no longer overwrite a task’s current status. * Completed tasks are now also removed during maintenance cleanup.

items.title: filer: resolve the collection a bucket delete drops
items.body: ## Summary A bucket delete dropped the collection named after the bucket, assuming bucket name is collection name. With a collection rule the write path already honors, that assumption breaks two ways: - deleting a bucket pointed at a dedicated custom collection left the collection behind as orphaned volumes; - deleting a bucket *named after* a collection other buckets resolve to removed the shared collection's volumes while their filer entries survived — LIST still returns the keys, GET fails. The delete now resolves the collection through the same rule chain the write path uses (`MatchStorageRule` on the bucket path, falling back to the bucket name) and drops it only when no other bucket resolves there too. items.title: Rust volume server: a cancelled VolumeCopy keeps running (Go aborts), leaking memory and mounting orphan volumes
items.body:
## Problem

In the Rust volume server, `VolumeCopy` does its work in a detached
`tokio::spawn` and reports progress with the send error discarded. Nothing
observes the client going away. When the caller cancels the RPC — which
`weed-admin`'s batch balance does routinely, starting far more copies than it
finishes — the server keeps streaming the whole volume from the source, writes
it to disk, and **mounts it** at the end.

The Go implementation does the opposite: it runs the copy inline in the handler
and aborts as soon as `stream.Send` fails.

This is separate from #11179 (unbounded redb index cache). That one is a cache
sizing problem; this is work that outlives its request.

## Version

- `weed-volume 0.1.0`, built from master (`283c6b886`, includes 4.45)
- `cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --no-default-features`
- Linux 7.1.x, x86-64, 16 instances, `--index=redb`, `replication=000`

## The difference

**Go** — `weed/server/volume_grpc_copy.go:154`. The progress callback returns
`false` when the send fails, which aborts the transfer:

```go
if sendErr = stream.Send(copyResponse); sendErr != nil {
    return false
}
```

**Rust** — `seaweed-volume/src/server/grpc_server.rs`:

```rust
// :1398  the whole copy runs here, detached; no JoinHandle is kept
tokio::spawn(async move {
    ...
    // :5083 (copy_file_from_source) progress send; the error is discarded, so a
    // dropped receiver does not stop the loop
    let _ = tx.send(Ok(VolumeCopyResponse { .. })).await;
    ...
    // :1553  the orphaned task mounts the volume even though nobody asked for it
    store.mount_volume(vid, &vol_info.collection, selected_disk_type)
    ...
});
// :1582  the client only ever holds the receiving end
let stream = ReceiverStream::new(rx);
```

Dropping the client stream drops `rx`, so `tx.send` starts returning `Err`.
Every send site uses `let _ =`. There is no `is_closed()` check, no `select!` on
cancellation, and no `AbortHandle`, so the task runs to completion regardless.

## Evidence

**Growth tracks abandoned copies, not bytes copied.**

Seven minutes of ordinary `weed-admin` balance activity on an idle cluster:

```
60 move stage: copying     <- copies started
10 move stage: moved       <- copies completed
```

One volume server's cgroup `anon` went **236 MB -> 487 MB (+251 MB)** and stayed
there. ~50 abandoned copies, ~5 MB each.

**Copies that complete normally do not do this.** Same cluster, same binary,
driving `volume.copy` by hand and letting each finish:

| test | result |
|---|---|
| 4 x complete copy of a 2.1 GB volume, deleted between | +9 MB anon total |
| 1 x complete copy of a 2.1 GB volume | +27 MB anon |
| 2.93 GiB of multipart S3 writes | +11 MB anon across all 16 instances |

So neither bulk transfer nor write traffic explains it; only the abandoned
copies do.

**It is retained, not in use.** An instance that reached 1627 MB `anon` with
`file` at 0 MB returned to **18 MB** on restart.

**It ends in a wedge, not a crash.** With `MemoryHigh=1500M` and a heap that is
~100% anonymous, the kernel forces reclaim that can never succeed. The process
stops serving, stays `active` to systemd with `NRestarts=0`, and
`memory.events` reports `max 0 oom 0` — no kill, no restart, no signal. We had
five instances in that state in one day before tracing it here.

## Also: orphaned copies leave mounted duplicates

Because the orphaned task calls `mount_volume` at the end, the destination
registers a volume the caller never took delivery of. Under `replication=000`
that shows up as one volume id on two servers. We finished a maintenance window
with three (`71`, `329`, `1760`) plus one seen earlier, including a 617 MB
`gitlab-data` volume whose two copies were byte-identical (`.dat` and `.idx`
md5s matched) and **both writable** — two writes routed to different servers
would have diverged them.

The balancer notices the mess without being able to name the cause:

```
volume 329 is left readonly on 10.0.0.1:8081: failed to delete the incomplete
copy on 10.0.0.1:8083 ...; delete that copy, then re-run the move
```

## Suggested fix

Make cancellation reach the task. Either of:

1. **Stop on a closed channel** — the smallest change, and it mirrors Go's
   semantics exactly. Check the result of `tx.send(...)` in
   `copy_file_from_source` and return an error when it fails; optionally also
   test `tx.is_closed()` between chunks so a copy with no progress reports still
   notices.
2. **Tie the task to the request** — keep the `JoinHandle` (or a
   `CancellationToken` / `DropGuard`) and abort when the response stream drops,
   which additionally covers the phases between file transfers.

Either way `mount_volume` should not run for a copy whose caller is gone, and
the partial files plus `.note` should be cleaned up on that path the same way
they are on error.

## What I could not test

A direct "cancel the client mid-transfer and watch the destination finish"
demonstration — the cluster lock was held by `weed-admin` whenever I tried, and
I was unwilling to stop it on a production cluster. The evidence above is the
code comparison plus the correlation between abandoned copies and retained
memory; the causal chain from cancellation to orphaned mount is read from the
source rather than observed end to end.

Happy to test a patch.
