items.title: Lazily-created remote-mount entries carry no TTL and accumulate without bound
items.body:
All references are to `master` @ `db5a086d0` (4.41).

## Problem

Under a lazy remote mount, filer entries are created on demand: `maybeLazyFetchFromRemote` on a miss in `FindEntry` (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote.go:30-117`) and `maybeLazyListFromRemote` on a directory listing (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:32-173`). Both create remote-only mappings — a path pointing at an object in the remote store — and neither sets `TtlSec`, so it stays `0` and nothing ever expires them.

They therefore accumulate one entry per distinct object ever touched, and are never reclaimed. On one of our filers that is currently **11,142,152 entries, growing by roughly 330,000/day**, with no upper bound short of the object count of the bucket.

The mount's own cache TTL does not help: `ListingCacheTtlSeconds` only decides how often a directory is re-listed from the remote (`filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:60-76`), and re-listing an existing entry takes the merge path at `:107-120`, which updates it. Nothing removes anything.

This is a real operational ceiling for anyone fronting cloud storage with a shared filer store. The entries are trivially reconstructible — the remote is authoritative, and a filer that lacks an entry re-derives it on the next access via exactly the code that created it.

## Why plain TTL is the right mechanism

The filer already has expiry machinery that does precisely what a cache wants, and — importantly — the *plain* TTL path never touches the remote:

- `FindEntry`: `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry(ctx, entry)` then `ErrNotFound` (`weed/filer/filer.go:434-437`);
- `doListDirectoryEntries`: expired entries collected at `:473-476` and deleted via `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry` at `:496-500`.

Both go to the store and nothing else. Neither reaches `doDeleteEntryMetaAndData`, so `maybeDeleteFromRemote` — which is gated on `!isFromOtherCluster` inside it (`weed/filer/filer_delete_entry.go:144-152`) — is not on that code path at all. Expiring a cached entry **cannot** propagate a delete to the remote object.

Worth having on the record: the S3-lifecycle branch a few lines above behaves differently. It calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, entry, true, false, nil)` (`filer.go:429` and `:492`) with `isFromOtherCluster: false`, so it *does* reach `maybeDeleteFromRemote` and *does* propagate. Whatever is decided here, those two expiry paths are not interchangeable for remote-mounted content.

No new job, no sweep, no schedule — the reclamation is already written.

## Two things have to be fixed first

### 1. `Crtime` is stamped with the remote object's mtime

Both creation sites set `Crtime` to the remote mtime, not to the creation time:

- `filer_lazy_remote.go:84-95` — `mtime := time.Unix(remoteEntry.RemoteMtime, 0)`, then `Mtime: mtime, Crtime: mtime`;
- `filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:137-146` — same, defaulting to `time.Now()` only when `RemoteMtime` is absent.

The expiry check is `Crtime + TtlSec < now`. Stamping a TTL as the code stands would expire every object older than the TTL window the instant its entry is created. And in `FindEntry` the expiry branch `return`s at `filer.go:436`, before the lazy-fetch fallback at `:440-446` — so the caller gets `ErrNotFound` for an object that demonstrably exists in the remote. The next request re-creates the entry, which is immediately expired again: objects would alternate 200/404 forever.

So `Crtime` has to mean "when this entry was created", with `Mtime` keeping the remote mtime. That split is arguably just correct on its own merits, independent of TTLs — `Crtime` is currently reporting a fact about the remote object rather than about the entry, and `entryInitialAtime` (`filer.go:395-400`) already prefers `Mtime` where the distinction matters.

### 2. Expiring a directory's last child can delete the remote prefix

This one I did not expect, and it is the reason I am opening an issue rather than a PR.

The entry deletion itself is store-only, as above. But `doListDirectoryEntries` does not stop there — when the expiry pass leaves no valid entries it calls `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` (`filer.go:502-507`), and that path *does* propagate:

- `IsDirectoryEmpty` (`filer.go:585-592`) calls `f.Store.ListDirectoryPrefixedEntries` directly, bypassing `maybeLazyListFromRemote` — so it sees only the local store and reports the directory empty even though every object is still sitting in the remote;
- it then calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, dirEntry, false, false, nil)` (`filer.go:573-574`) — `isFromOtherCluster: false`;
- for a directory entry, `maybeDeleteFromRemote` calls `client.RemoveDirectory` (`filer_lazy_remote.go:139-148`);
- `RemoveDirectory` on S3 (`weed/remote_storage/s3/s3_storage_client.go:429`) and GCS (`weed/remote_storage/gcs/gcs_storage_client.go:222`) lists the prefix and **deletes every object under it**.

The only guard is the depth check at `filer.go:550-555`, which protects `/buckets/<bucket>` but nothing below it. So a TTL on lazy entries, added naively, turns "this directory's cached metadata went cold" into "wipe that prefix from the bucket".

It is latent today only because lazy entries carry `TtlSec: 0` and so never reach that code. (The same `isFromOtherCluster: false` call is reachable from the scheduled empty-folder cleaner — `weed/filer/empty_folder_cleanup/empty_folder_cleaner.go:360` — which suggests the interaction between remote mounts and empty-directory cleanup deserves a look regardless of this proposal.)

The fix that fits the existing design is to make `maybeDeleteFromRemote` decline to remove a directory whose emptiness was never confirmed against the remote, or to skip `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` when the entries were reclaimed by cache expiry rather than deleted by a client. I would rather agree the shape with you than pick one.

## Proposal

Three parts:

1. `Crtime` = creation time at both lazy-creation sites, `Mtime` unchanged. Small and independently defensible.
2. Do not propagate a remote directory removal that originates from cache expiry (see above).
3. Give lazy-created entries a configurable TTL.

For (3), the machinery already exists and I would rather reuse it than add a flag: `FilerConf.PathConf.ttl` (`weed/pb/filer.proto:758`) is already parsed by `needle.ReadTTL` and turned into the entry's `TtlSec` on the upload path (`weed/server/filer_server_handlers_write.go:289-295`). Having the two lazy-creation sites do the same `f.FilerConf.MatchStorageRule(path).GetTtl()` lookup would mean a lazy mount is configured with the command that already exists:

```
fs.configure -locationPrefix=/buckets/mybucket/ -ttl=7d -apply
```

no new proto field, no new flag, and it composes with everything else `filer.conf` already scopes per path. The alternative — a `remote.mount -entryTTL` flag mirroring `-listingCacheTTL` (`weed/shell/command_remote_mount.go:73,93`) — keeps the setting next to the mount it belongs to, at the cost of a second place TTLs come from. I lean towards the `filer.conf` route but have no strong attachment.

## Related

Under a store that expires values natively, there is a second half to this. `redis2`'s directory index leaks a member for every entry whose value key expires, because the listing loop only cleans up on the logical-expiry branch and not on the not-found branch that TTL entries actually take — so TTL-based reclamation frees the values but not the index. Fix in #10735. The two changes compose: TTLs here, and a store that stays clean when they fire.

Background: #8391, #8454, #8522, #8568 are the lazy remote-mount work this builds on. Happy to implement all three parts if the approach sounds right — particularly keen for a steer on (2) before writing anything.

items.title: redis2: pipeline entry reads when listing a directory
items.body: # What problem are we solving? Supersedes #4508 by @Woellchen, which went stale and no longer applies to the redis2 store on master. Thanks for the original idea! `ListDirectoryEntries` in the redis2 store reads every member with its own `GET`, so listing a page of 1024 entries costs 1024 round trips to Redis. When Redis sits on another host, every listing pays that latency once per entry. # How are we solving the problem? The listing fetches the values in pipelined batches of 128, one batch each time the loop reaches it, and walks the replies in member order through the same decode step `FindEntry` uses. Every reply keeps its own error, so the loop is otherwise unchanged: - a missing value still goes through the orphaned index member cleanup and is skipped - a logically expired entry is still deleted and skipped - any other error still ends the listing at that member and is returned - limits, the start file name and super large directories behave as before Why batches of 128: a full 1024 entry page takes 8 round trips instead of 1024. Some callers list with `limit` set to `math.MaxInt32` and stop after the first entry they want, for example the latest version recompute in `applyRecomputeLatest`. With one pipeline per call they would read every value in the directory; with batches they read at most 128. It also keeps any single pipeline small next to the read timeout. Kept from #4508: the pipelined `GET`s from its `FindEntries`. Left out: - Writing entries with `Set(..., 0)`. That dropped the native Redis TTL, so expired values would stay in Redis until someone read or listed them. - The pipelined insert, update and delete paths and the renames. The listing does not need them, and their error messages wrapped the pipeline's `err` instead of the failed command's error. On the review question in #4508 about a first batch where every entry has expired: #4508 only moved `lastFileName` on live entries, so an all expired batch came back with an empty name. Here `lastFileName` still moves past every member, as on master, and expired entries are still deleted and skipped. A page made up only of expired or missing members still returns no entries, as on master, and `ListEntries` stops there. Refilling such a page would be a separate change. # How is the PR tested? Three new tests in the gated redis2 suite: - live, missing and expired members in one page: only the live ones are listed, in order, and the rest leave the index - 130 entries with the member right after the first batch missing: the other 129 are listed and the index is repaired - a value of the wrong type: the listing stops there with an error after the entries before it The first and third also pass on master, so the behaviour they check has not changed. The second uses the new batch size constant. Run against Redis 8.0.5: ``` cd weed go build ./filer/redis2/ && go vet ./filer/redis2/ RUN_REDIS_TESTS=1 REDIS_ADDR=:6379 go test ./filer/redis2/ -count=1 -v ``` By hand I also listed a 300 entry directory through a three node Redis Cluster, with the keys spread over all three masters and missing and expired members mixed in. The 206 live entries came back in order and the index matched. Timing at the store level (`ListDirectoryEntries` called directly, range over 7 runs) from a client to a standalone Redis on another host over the LAN, minimum PING round trip about 0.5 ms: | | master | this PR | |---|---|---| | list 1000 entries, limit 1024 | 1.3 to 1.7 s | 17 to 18 ms | | limit `math.MaxInt32`, callback stops after the first entry | 2.5 ms | 2.5 to 3.5 ms | # Checks - [x] I have added unit tests if possible. - [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging. - [ ] All AI code review comments have been addressed. No more comments to fix if reviewed again. Reviewer may request additional gemini and copilot reviews. # Checks for AI generated PRs - [ ] I have reviewed every line of code. - [x] The PR is kept as minimum as possible. Large PRs would not be accepted. --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Directory listings now skip missing or expired entries while preserving the order of remaining entries, and remove stale entries from the listing index. * Listings spanning multiple fetch batches continue to handle missing entries correctly. * If an entry cannot be read because of a Redis error, listing stops at that entry and reports the error and its name. * **Performance** * Directory entries are fetched in batches, reducing individual Redis reads for larger listings.

items.title: volume server: split volume_copy into phases and type the delete-after-status gate
items.body: ## Problem `VolumeCopy` in the Rust volume server was a single ~400-line handler, and two invariants were held by convention only: - An existing local replica may be deleted only **after** the source answered `ReadVolumeFileStatus` (Go: `weed/server/volume_grpc_copy.go:VolumeCopy`, "the delete is deferred until ReadVolumeFileStatus below proves the source holds the volume"). In Rust, only the order of the statements guaranteed it. - The pre-copy delete and the failed-copy rollback must both pass `keep_remote_data=true`, because a remote-tier copy's `.vif` points at the same cloud object as the source replica. Only a comment in the rollback pointing back at the first call kept them in sync. ## Change `volume_copy` is now a ~60-line orchestrator over named phases: - `connect_to_copy_source` → `SourceVolumeStatus::fetch` → `delete_existing_replica` → `plan_copy_destination` → `CopyDestination::write_note` - then a spawned `VolumeCopyJob::run`: `preallocate_dat` → `transfer_files` → `finish_copied_files` → `mount_and_reply`, with `cleanup_failed_copy` on error. `SourceVolumeStatus` wraps the `ReadVolumeFileStatusResponse` in a child module with a private field, so `fetch` is its only constructor, and `delete_existing_replica` takes `&SourceVolumeStatus`, so the delete cannot be called before the status RPC. This is checked at compile time: constructing one elsewhere fails with E0423. Both deletes go through one `delete_replica_keep_remote` helper. ## What did NOT change This is a pure refactor. Call order, every `Status` code and message, the cancellation checks (#11188), throttling and progress reports, the master-config `select!`, lock scopes, and cleanup-on-failure behave exactly as before. At the top of each method, locals are bound with the original names so the moved bodies stay byte-identical. ## Reviewing Most of the diff is moved code: git diff --color-moved=zebra --color-moved-ws=allow-indentation-change (324 lines moved out, 366 moved in; 40 really removed, 158 really added.) Plain `--color-moved` won't match the re-indented task body. ## Verified - `cargo test` (all targets): 680 + 5 + 1 + 32 pass, including the existing VolumeCopy cancellation and rollback tests, unchanged. - `cargo clippy --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --check`: nothing new. - Go integration suite `test/volume_server/grpc` with `VOLUME_SERVER_IMPL=rust`: all 12 VolumeCopy / MixedBalance / VolumeMove tests pass. `get_or_head_handler_inner` (handlers.rs), the other half of this item, is left for a separate PR. Part of franchb/seaweedfs#10 (P3 simplification: volume_copy / get_or_head_handler_inner). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Volume copies now verify the source volume is available before replacing an existing destination. * Copies select a disk with sufficient free space for the required files, with different space checks for local and remote-backed volumes. * If a client disconnects after a copy is mounted but before receiving the response, the mounted replica is cleaned up while remote data is preserved. * Copy operations continue to respect cancellation during source reads, transfer throttling, and master configuration lookup.

items.title: filer: evict remote-cached objects under storage pressure
items.body: ## Summary Remote-mounted objects cache to ordinary local volumes on read, but nothing evicts them when the disk fills: failed fills leave tombstoned garbage, the mount collection loses writable volumes, and every later read streams from remote forever (reproduced locally with 2 nodes and 5 x 16MB objects against 64MB of volume capacity). This adds pressure-driven eviction at the filer level, where the metadata knows which chunks are safely re-fetchable. - `filer.IsEvictableRemoteEntry` / `ListEvictableRemoteEntries`: entry is a candidate only when remote-backed, synced (`LastLocalSyncTsNs >= remote mtime`), and holding local chunks - never dirty or pending-upload content. Ordered by `LastLocalSyncTsNs`, oldest cached first. - `FilerServer.uncacheRemoteEntry` applies the same state transition as `remote.uncache` (clear chunks, reset sync ts) through the normal entry lock + `CreateEntry` mutation path. - Reactive: a cache fill that fails with a capacity error launches a reclaim pass (evict oldest until the object fits) before the read falls back to remote streaming. Passes coalesce via TryLock, so a write-failure storm does not queue mount traversals. - Proactive: a filer janitor runs the same pass when any volume-server disk crosses `-filer.remoteCacheEvictThreshold` (default 0.9, 0 disables), evicting down to ~85% of that threshold for hysteresis. - Reclaim: the pass flushes the deletion queue synchronously and triggers a master vacuum, so evicted chunks and orphaned partial-fill garbage return to the filesystem promptly instead of waiting for the next auto-vacuum. - Metric: `seaweedfs_remote_cache_evicted_total`. Enterprise cache volumes are unaffected: this only drops chunks of entries with remote-mount metadata in ordinary volumes, and never touches remote-tiered volume needle data. #### Test plan - [x] `weed/filer` unit tests: eligibility matrix, oldest-first ordering, min-age cutoff, dirty/remote-only skips, subdirectory recursion - [x] `TestRemoteCacheEvictUnderPressure` (test/s3/remote_cache): self- contained two-mini cluster, 2 x 32MB volumes vs 5 x 16MB objects; asserts the oldest entry is evicted, garbage is vacuumed, and a re-read re-caches - [x] Live two-node repro validated: wedged cache (272MB garbage, zero live data) self-heals on the next read - [ ] CI Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added automatic reclamation of locally cached remote files when volume disk usage reaches a configurable threshold. Eligible files are evicted oldest-first; the default threshold is 90%, and setting it to 0 disables eviction. * Evicted files remain available remotely and can be fetched locally again when needed. * When remote-cache capacity is exhausted, the system can reclaim local cache space to make room for new cached files. * **Bug Fixes** * Improved cache tracking so locally modified files are not mistaken for unchanged remote copies during eviction.

items.title: filer: option to store system metadata logs in their own collection
items.body: ## Problem The filer's internal system metadata log (`/topics/.system/log`) chunks are assigned to the filer's **default collection** (`-collection` flag). In multi-filer deployments where that default is empty (`""`), every restart flap, full-sync, or event-buffered flush grows the default collection with system chunks that are indistinguishable from user data in `collection.list`. This makes the `default` collection balloon silently over time and badly confuses orphan analysis: operators see gigabytes in `""` and cannot tell what is real user data (misrouted writes) vs. internal log churn — and are afraid to clean anything. ## What this PR does Give the internal metadata log its own collection when the operator asks for one, without changing where user data goes: - New optional knobs, read in `NewFiler` so both `weed filer` and `weed server -filer` honour them: - `filer.options.metaLog.collection` — collection for the internal log chunks (default `""` => exactly today's behaviour: log follows the filer's `-collection` flag; fully backward compatible). - `filer.options.metaLog.replication` — optional replication override for the log volumes. - Resolution is a small helper (`metaLogCollectionFor` / `metaLogReplicationFor`): explicit override first, then the filer default, then a storage rule matched on the log path. - Scaffold `filer.toml` documents the new knobs under `[filer.options]`. ## Key code subtlety `f.metaLogCollection` currently has **double duty**: it is both the log's assignment target (`assignAndUpload`) *and* the "filer's default collection" reference in the `bucketCollection()` delete guard — the check that stops a bucket delete from dropping a collection shared with non-bucket paths. Overloading the same field for the log destination would change that guard's semantics. So this PR introduces separate `metaLogTargetCollection` / `metaLogTargetReplication` fields, and extends the delete guard to protect the redirected meta-log collection the same way it already protects the filer default: a bucket that happens to resolve to the meta-log collection must not drop it either, because internal log volumes live there. ## Testing `go test -race ./weed/filer/` green, including: - `TestMetaLogCollectionResolution` — full precedence chain (override / filer default / matched rule) incl. the backward-compatible unset case. - `TestMetaLogReplicationResolution` — same for replication. - `TestViperReadsMetaLogOverrides` — pins the exact viper keys. - `TestBucketCollectionKeepsMetaLogTargetCollection` — deleting a bucket that resolves to the redirected meta-log collection issues **no** collection drop. - The existing `TestDeleteBucket*` guards unaffected. Build: `go build ./...` green. gofmt clean. ## Related Independent of https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/pull/11550 (durable deletion ledger) — no file overlap in the functional paths, either can merge first. Together they cut the two sources of post-flap junk in the `default` collection: - #11550 stops orphaned **user chunks** leaking when a filer crash loses its RAM-only deletion queue - this PR stops the internal **metadata log** from living in the default collection in the first place --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added optional collection and replication settings for filer metadata logs. When unset, the filer’s defaults and matching storage rules continue to apply. * Documented that changing the metadata-log collection does not move existing log chunks or alter their volume references. * **Bug Fixes** * Bucket deletion now preserves collections used for filer metadata logs. Other collections retain their existing deletion behavior.

items.title: s3api: don't delete chunks when CreateEntry outcome is ambiguous
items.body: ## Summary Fixes #11366. When a PUT's `CreateEntry` fails with a transport error (`Unavailable`, `Canceled`, `DeadlineExceeded`), the filer may have applied the write anyway — e.g. the object-owner filer was restarting and the response was lost. `putToFiler` treated `entryCreated == false` as proof of failure and tombstoned the uploaded chunks via `deleteOrphanedChunks`, leaving the live filer entry pointing at deleted needles. Reads keep working only because they pass `readDeleted=true`, until vacuum reclaims the needle and the object turns into delayed data loss. Commits: - **`filerErrorToS3Error`: ambiguous transport errors → `ServiceUnavailable` (503)** instead of a permanent 4xx, so clients retry rather than give up. - **Verify before deleting orphaned chunks**: on a failed create, `putToFiler` now looks the entry up first — - entry stored with the same chunks → the write landed, treat it as successful; - lookup unverifiable → keep the chunks (vacuum reclaims true orphans); - confirmed absent → delete the orphans as before. - **Regression tests** for all three cases (`s3api_object_handlers_put_ambiguous_test.go`), with a fake filer that applies the entry and still returns `Unavailable`, plus a fake volume server that records deleted file ids. - **Volume servers (Go + Rust, mirrored)**: count reads served from deleted needles under a `readDeletedNeedle` handler label — the observable signal of the dangling-pointer condition before vacuum makes it a 404. #### Test plan - [x] `go test ./weed/s3api` — all pass, including the 3 new regression tests - [x] `go test ./weed/storage` - [x] `go build ./weed/s3api ./weed/storage ./weed/stats` - [x] `cargo check` + `cargo test` (read/deleted-related) in `seaweed-volume` --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved S3 upload handling for ambiguous create errors by preserving uploaded data while the result is verified. * Requests affected by cancellations, timeouts, or unavailable services now return a service-unavailable error. * **Monitoring** * Added metrics for reads of deleted volume entries across volume servers. * **Tests** * Added coverage for successful, failed, stale, and unverifiable ambiguous upload outcomes.

items.title: ec_vacuum: superseded EC shard generation never deleted after a successful 2PC switch — unbounded disk growth
items.body:
Environment:

SeaweedFS Enterprise, two independent clusters: 4.44 (production) and 4.47 — latest available — (dev)
Topology: 5 racks × 2 volume servers (10 total, single disk each), 020 replication, EC 6+4
Deployed via the official Helm chart


Summary:
The ec_vacuum job type's generation-switch mechanism (executor_2pc.go) successfully vacuums garbage out of EC volumes and commits a new, smaller shard generation — but never deletes the superseded generation's files afterward. Every successful vacuum run adds disk usage instead of reclaiming it. This reproduces identically on both 4.44 and 4.47, so it isn't fixed in the latest release.

Reproduction (production, 4.44):

Volume 1656, EC vacuum ran and reported full success:

```
executor_2pc.go:77   ec vacuum 2PC switch volume=1656 old=3 new=4 targets=10
executor_2pc.go:90   2PC stage shards OK; entering Prepare fan-out across 10 targets
executor_2pc.go:133  2PC Prepare OK on all 10 targets; entering Commit fan-out
executor_2pc.go:179  2PC switch COMPLETE volume=1656 active_version=4
executor.go:323      ec vacuum shard verification ok for volume 1656: 10/10 shards present across 10 nodes
```

Real garbage was reclaimed — shard 0 shrank from 301MB to 157MB (48%). But both generations are present on disk right now, on every one of the 10 shard-holding nodes:

```
backups-postgres_1656.ec00.v3   315,621,376 bytes   Sep 27 14:27   ← superseded, still present
backups-postgres_1656.ec00.v4   164,626,432 bytes   Sep 28 08:29   ← new active generation
```

(Same pattern confirmed independently on volume 1657: .ec00.v3 300MB alongside new .v4 151MB.) No VolumeEcShardsUnmount/VolumeEcShardsDelete call, nor any teardown/cleanup log line, appears anywhere in the worker or admin logs for either volume, before or after the switch.

Scale of impact: on dev (4.47), a single volume-server node accumulated 7,138 orphaned generation files (~98.8 GiB) in under 6 days of cluster uptime — roughly 21% of that node's total used disk. Production (4.44, 30 days uptime) has accumulated on the order of several TB cluster-wide from the same cause. This is not a slow edge case; it's the dominant source of disk growth on both clusters.

Related but distinct — false-positive verification failure on fully-deleted volumes: separately, ec_vacuum on a volume where 100% of needles are already deleted (confirmed via count: 77 deleted: 77 in the worker log, source .dat size 8 bytes) reports the switch as COMPLETE, then immediately fails verification with 0/10 shards present, missing shard ids [0-9], NotFound from every single node:

```
executor_2pc.go:179  2PC switch COMPLETE volume=1494 active_version=7
executor.go:319      ERROR: ec vacuum shard verification failed for volume 1494: EC shard set incomplete: 0/10 shards present ... NotFound 
```

(all 10 nodes)
The master's live topology confirms the volume is genuinely gone (not a race — no trace anywhere, no files on any node), consistent with a fully-emptied volume being correctly retired. But the error is indistinguishable from a real failure, and with retry_limit: 1 these volumes get permanently stuck rather than cleanly recognized as "nothing left to store."

items.title: [BUG REPORT] S3: filer metadata can reference a tombstoned chunk — masked by readDeleted=true, becomes silent data loss after vacuum
items.body:
````markdown
### Describe the bug

An S3 object's filer entry can point at a chunk that has been deleted
(tombstoned) in the volume index. Because the filer read path unconditionally
appends `readDeleted=true`, the object stays fully readable (HEAD/GET 200 with
the original size and Last-Modified), so the inconsistency is invisible to
clients. Once the volume is vacuumed, the tombstoned needle is physically
reclaimed and the object suddenly returns 404 — silent, delayed data loss.

Observed on one object, shortly after an S3 `PUT` returned 400 while the object
was nevertheless created (the filer entry's mtime matches the failing PUT).
Both objects referenced below are still readable at the time of writing.

### Environment

- SeaweedFS 4.47, volume server built with `-tags=5BytesOffset` (large-disk
  build; `.idx` records are 17 bytes: needleId(8) + offset(5) + size(4))
- 3-replica volume (`ReplicaPlacement:020`), S3 API
- Writer: rclone v1.69.1

### Evidence

#### 1. `volume.fsck -findMissingChunksInFiler` reports the chunks as missing on all 3 replicas (reproducible)

```
$ volume.fsck -collection mybucket-20260915 -volumeId 166145293 -findMissingChunksInFiler
total 25 directories, 14707013 files
/buckets/mybucket-20260915/18/object-a.eml
/buckets/mybucket-20260915/18/object-b.eml
/buckets/mybucket-20260915/18/object-a.eml
/buckets/mybucket-20260915/18/object-b.eml
/buckets/mybucket-20260915/18/object-a.eml
/buckets/mybucket-20260915/18/object-b.eml
```

Each path is printed once per replica (the check is per-replica and does not
deduplicate), i.e. the chunk is missing on all three.

#### 2. Reading through the filer succeeds; reading the same fid directly from every replica 404s

```
# via the filer / S3 path -> 200 with the full object
$ curl -I "http://10.0.0.20:15672/buckets/mybucket-20260915/18/object-a.eml"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 109036
Last-Modified: Tue, 15 Sep 2026 10:38:03 GMT
Server: SeaweedFS 8000GB 4.47

# the fid from fs.meta.cat, read directly from each replica -> 404
$ curl -I "http://10.0.0.11:8013/166145293,0643b039c91ef08cc9"
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Server: SeaweedFS Volume 8000GB 4.47
$ curl -I "http://10.0.0.12:8023/166145293,0643b039c91ef08cc9"
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Server: SeaweedFS Volume 8000GB 4.47
$ curl -I "http://10.0.0.13:8027/166145293,0643b039c91ef08cc9"
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Server: SeaweedFS Volume 8000GB 4.47
```

#### 3. The `.idx` shows the needle written and then tombstoned (later record wins)

```
$ stat -c '%s' mybucket-20260915_166145293.idx
7551536          # 7551536 / 17 = 444208 -> 5BytesOffset build

$ python3 idx_dump.py mybucket-20260915_166145293.idx 643b039c9
275037  643b039c9  off=16974881328  size=109048
275039  643b039c9  off=16974996632  size=-1  DEL
```

The later record is `TombstoneFileSize` (-1). `doLoading`
(`weed/storage/needle_map_memory.go:37-58`) applies records in file order, so the
needle ends up absent from the in-memory map and every normal read returns 404.
This matches the fsck output — the fsck report is correct, not a false positive.

#### 4. `readDeleted=true` shows the data is physically still present

```
$ curl -I "http://10.0.0.13:8027/166145293,0643b039c91ef08cc9?readDeleted=true"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 109036
Last-Modified: Tue, 15 Sep 2026 10:38:03 GMT
Server: SeaweedFS Volume 8000GB 4.47
```

#### 5. S3 gateway access log around the write

```
10.0.0.60 - - [15/Sep/2026:18:37:59 +0800] http s3.example.internal:8333 404 "HEAD /mybucket-20260915/18/object-a.eml HTTP/1.1" 647 0.002 238 0 - upstream=127.0.0.1:3333 "-" - "rclone/v1.69.1"
10.0.0.60 - - [15/Sep/2026:18:38:03 +0800] http s3.example.internal:8333 400 "PUT /mybucket-20260915/18/object-a.eml?x-id=PutObject HTTP/1.1" 109848 0.049 561 321 - upstream=127.0.0.1:3333 "-" - "rclone/v1.69.1"
10.0.0.60 - - [15/Sep/2026:18:38:07 +0800] http s3.example.internal:8333 200 "HEAD /mybucket-20260915/18/object-a.eml HTTP/1.1" 647 0.002 453 0 - upstream=127.0.0.1:3333 "-" - "rclone/v1.69.1"
```

The filer entry's mtime is `1789468683` = `2026-09-15 18:38:03 +0800` — the same
second as the PUT that returned 400. The PUT's request length (109848 bytes,
including headers) is the whole object (~109036 bytes), i.e. the server received
the complete object and still answered 400.

### Root cause analysis

1. **Filer reads always append `readDeleted=true`.**
   `weed/filer/stream.go:527` (`ChunkStreamReader.fetchChunkToBuffer`) and
   `weed/filer/filechunk_manifest.go:421` build every chunk URL with
   `AppendQueryParameter(urlString, "readDeleted", "true")`; the volume server
   honors it (`weed/server/volume_server_handlers_read.go:180`,
   `weed/storage/volume_read.go:36,133`). As long as the volume has not been
   vacuumed, a metadata entry that points at a tombstoned needle is served
   normally, so the inconsistency has no client-visible symptom.

2. **The write path is not atomic and its rollback is best-effort.**
   `putToFiler` uploads chunks, verifies checksums, then creates the filer entry
   (`weed/s3api/s3api_object_handlers_put.go`). Chunks are deleted only when
   `entryCreated == false` (:993-1003). The post-create rollback calls `rmObject`
   and only logs a failure (:940-948). If that rollback only partially succeeds
   (data deleted, metadata left behind), the dangling reference persists with no
   retry or compensation.

3. **Nothing reconciles the two views.** There is no background check between
   filer metadata and volume needle maps; `volume.fsck -findMissingChunksInFiler`
   detects the state but is manual, and `volume.check.disk` only compares
   replicas against each other.

`readDeleted=true` is presumably deliberate, to tolerate the in-flight window
between tombstoning a needle and removing the metadata entry. The problem is
that the resulting state is unbounded and unobservable.

### Impact

Silent, delayed data loss. The object remains listable and readable until
`volume.vacuum` (or any compaction) reclaims the tombstoned needle; after that
every read returns 404, with no warning beforehand. A client that received a 400
for its PUT can still observe a "successful" object afterwards.

### Suggested fixes

- Make the write/rollback path transactional, or add an explicit compensation
  step with retries; do not swallow rollback errors.
- Make the `readDeleted` fallback observable: log/emit a metric when a chunk is
  served from a deleted needle, since that indicates filer metadata and the
  volume index disagree. Optionally bound how long it is tolerated.
- Add a background consistency check between filer metadata and volume
  tombstones with alerting, or surface it in `volume.fsck` as a distinct,
  actionable category.

### How to inspect `.idx` locally (5BytesOffset builds)

```python
import sys
d = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
N = 17  # needleId(8) + offset(5) + size(4); plain builds use 16 with offset at bytes[8:12]
assert len(d) % N == 0, f"size={len(d)} not a multiple of {N}"
for i in range(0, len(d), N):
    r = d[i:i+N]
    nid = int.from_bytes(r[0:8], 'big')
    off = (r[11] | r[10]<<8 | r[9]<<16 | r[8]<<24 | r[12]<<32) * 8
    size = int.from_bytes(r[13:17], 'big', signed=True)
    print(f"{i//N}\t{nid:x}\toff={off}\tsize={size}\t{'DEL' if size < 0 else ''}")
```
````

items.title: filer: guard FoundationDB 100KB value limit and pack earlier
items.body: Fixes #11158 The filer stores an entry's chunk list as one FoundationDB value. FDB caps values at 100,000 bytes, but `UpdateEntry` checked the 10 MB transaction limit, and `MaybeManifestize` only folded at `ManifestBatch = 10000`. With default `-maxMB=4`, a few-GiB PutObject hit error 2103 before packing ran. ## Changes - FoundationDB store implements `ManifestBatcher` and returns 500. Other stores keep 10000. - Process-wide batch (`GetManifestBatch` / `SetManifestBatch`) is set from the default store in `SetStore` and advertised as `GetFilerConfiguration.manifest_batch`. - S3, mount, WebDAV, and `filer.copy` apply that field on handshake (`ApplyRemoteManifestBatch` ignores 0 so old filers keep 10000). - `MaybeManifestize` uses the process-wide batch. SSE chunks still skip packing. - `UpdateEntry` and `KvPut` reject `len(value) > 100000` *after* gzip and *before* `Transact`, with an error that names the value limit. `FDB_TRANSACTION_SIZE_LIMIT` is removed; directory delete still batches by entry count. - `cleanupChunks` (CreateEntry / UpdateEntry gRPC only) uses `ManifestizeOrKeepFlat`: on packing failure it deletes partial manifest blobs and continues with the flat list. `ObjectTransaction` PUT is unchanged (callers send a prepared list; current-tree S3 falls back to CreateEntry if the named guard fires). Single-pass packing at batch 500 and `-maxMB=4` still has a ~2 TiB ceiling; nested packing is out of scope. ## Tests - Unit tests for the batch API, wrapper/`SetStore`, fold-at-500, SSE skip, packing rollback, FDB value-size helper, and `GetFilerConfiguration`. - Existing `weed/filer` and `weed/s3api` manifest tests (still on `ManifestBatch = 10000`). - `cargo check --manifest-path seaweed-volume/Cargo.toml -p weed-volume` for the proto field. The FDB helper tests live in untagged files so they run without `libfdb_c`. Tagged store tests still need FoundationDB headers. --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **Bug Fixes** - Improved manifest processing reliability by preserving existing file chunks when folding fails. - Added cleanup for partially created manifest data, reducing the risk of orphaned storage. - Oversized metadata values are now rejected consistently before storage writes, with clearer size-limit errors. - Failed manifest operations continue to preserve a correct flat object representation. - **Performance** - Reduced manifest batch sizes to accommodate storage value limits and improve compatibility. - **Tests** - Added coverage for size validation, rollback, failure recovery, and manifest preservation.

items.title: master: don't let a dead KeepConnected handler close its successor's channel
items.body:
Fixes #10892.

The reporter's analysis was exactly right. When a client reconnects KeepConnected before the old handler has exited, `addClient` overwrites the map entry under the same client name. The old handler's deferred `deleteClient` then closes whatever channel the map holds under that name, which is the new, live stream's channel. A receive from a closed channel returns nil immediately and forever, and the send loop did not check `ok`, so it degenerated into `for { stream.Send(nil) }`: empty responses at wire speed, one core pinned on each end, until someone kills the TCP connection.

Reproduced against a live master by opening two KeepConnected streams with the same ClientAddress and canceling the first: the surviving stream received 5.5 million empty messages in two seconds. With this change it receives none and stays connected.

The fix is ownership: `deleteClient` closes the channel its own handler registered, and removes the map entry only if it still points to that channel. Closing under the write lock is safe because broadcasters send while holding the read lock and only to channels found in the map. This also closes the old handler's orphaned channel, whose drain goroutine used to leak, and the send loop now treats a closed channel as an exit rather than a message stream.

The cluster membership side of the same defer was already safe: `GroupMembers` refcounts overlapping registrations.

items.title: s3: an abort answered mid-part no longer leaves the upload completable
items.body:
Fixes #11024.

`PutObjectPartHandler` checks that `.uploads/<id>` still exists before it reads
the part body. An abort answered during that read removes the directory, and the
part write that follows re-creates it on its way to the filer: the part lands
with a 200 and the upload `ListMultipartUploads` no longer lists still completes
into an object.

Reproduced with the reporter's script on `weed mini` at 624deaf3a:

```
A) part in flight across the abort
  AbortMultipartUpload       -> 204 No Content
  UploadPart body sent       -> 200 OK
  ListMultipartUploads       -> 200 OK, 0 listed
  CompleteMultipartUpload    -> 200 OK
  HEAD object                -> 200 OK
```

The re-created directory is the tell. `createMultipartUpload` stamps the
destination object key on `.uploads/<id>`; the filer's implicit parent creation
does not, which is also why the upload stopped listing:

```
fs.meta.cat /buckets/probe/.uploads/325ffddd..._bd04f45a...
  "isDirectory": true,
  "extended": {},
```

Three commits:

1. UploadPart re-checks the upload after the part lands and, when the directory
   is one its own write resurrected, drops it along with the part and answers
   `NoSuchUpload`.
2. UploadPartCopy has the same window — the check runs before the bytes are
   copied. Aborting mid-copy of a 40MB source made 8 of 16 attempts completable;
   both the re-encryption and the raw-copy path now re-check.
3. CompleteMultipartUpload refuses a `.uploads/<id>` carrying no upload record.
   Posting a part straight to the filer under an unused upload id used to
   assemble an object out of it; it now answers `NoSuchUpload`. This also covers
   directories a pre-fix gateway left behind.

After, A) matches the control case, and the copy race stops at 0 of 16:

```
A) part in flight across the abort
  AbortMultipartUpload       -> 204 No Content
  UploadPart body sent       -> 404 Not Found NoSuchUpload
  ListMultipartUploads       -> 200 OK, 0 listed
  CompleteMultipartUpload    -> 404 Not Found NoSuchUpload
  HEAD object                -> 404 Not Found
```

Multipart upload, UploadPartCopy and their round trips still work (40MB in 5
parts, byte-identical back); `go test ./weed/s3api/...` passes. The cost is one
extra `LookupDirectoryEntry` per part write, against a request that already
carried the part's bytes.

Not changed: the second `CompleteMultipartUpload` on an already-completed id
answering 200. That one is deliberate — the completion path recognizes the
object it wrote for this upload id and replays the same result, so a client
whose response was lost can retry.

items.title: s3 lifecycle: share daily bucket walk and prune listings
items.body: ## Summary Fixes #11791 — the daily lifecycle pass invoked the bucket walk once per shard, so with the default 16 shards every pass listed the entire bucket tree 16 times against the filer. Three changes, one commit each: - **Share the daily bucket walk across shards.** Run() plans up to two shared walks per pass (one RecoveryView group, one steady-state group) and every covered shard awaits the same physical listing while keeping its own cursor and shard filtering. WalkerFunc now takes the shard set. - **Skip the .versions/ pre-pass on non-versioned buckets.** FilerListFunc receives the walk view; versioned buckets keep the two-pass walk while ordinary buckets list each directory once. items.title: filer: do not sweep children when deleting a folder non-recursively
items.body:
Fixes #10779

`doBatchDeleteFolderMetaAndData` lists a folder's children and returns `fail to delete non-empty folder` if it finds any, then calls `Store.DeleteFolderChildren` unconditionally. On the non-recursive path that bulk sweep has nothing legitimate to remove — it is only reached once the listing came back empty, so the only rows it can possibly delete are ones inserted after the check.

The S3 empty-folder cleaner deletes through exactly this path. An object written between the listing and the sweep loses its entry after the write was already acknowledged, and the failure is silent on both sides: the client has its 200, and the cleaner logs an ordinary `deleting empty folder`. The chunks leak too, because the cleaner passes `shouldDeleteChunks=false` and the empty listing collected nothing, so the needles stay on the volume unreferenced until someone runs `volume.fsck`.

The window is reachable on any workload that shards object keys over a small fixed set of shallow prefixes. A layout like `<prefix>/<3 chars>/<random>` spreads objects uniformly across a few thousand folders, so once the live object count drops below the folder count, nearly every delete empties a folder and nearly every write revives one that has been idle long enough to be queued for cleanup. The set of folders pending deletion and the set about to be written are then the same set, and a single run can log tens of thousands of folder deletions, each carrying the window.

ClickHouse hit exactly this in their stateless CI. Their S3 disk generates keys as `<prefix>/[a-z]{3}/[a-z]{29}`, and one job logged 34,819 folder deletions at a peak of 3,238/min. The symptom is `Object <key> in bucket <bucket> suddenly disappeared`, raised by `s3_check_objects_after_upload` doing a HEAD immediately after upload. They worked around it in ClickHouse/ClickHouse#114660 by pushing `empty_folder_cleanup_delay` out to 24h.

That workaround does not fix the bug. The delay changes how often the deletion runs, not what it does when it runs, so a long delay defers the problem rather than removing it.

The `.uploads` guard added in #10273 covered one subtree where this first surfaced. The window is not specific to multipart staging — every object folder has it.

## Fix

Sweep only when the delete is recursive, or when the whole-bucket shortcut skipped the listing and relies on the sweep to drop the table.

## Reproduction

A stress harness driving the cleaner's exact call against a concurrent writer, on a real `Filer` over leveldb2, destroyed 33 entries out of 105,521 creates across 7,554 folder deletions. End to end over S3 against a stock `weed server` in that CI's configuration, 9 objects were destroyed out of 456,762 PUTs, each loss matching a `deleting empty folder` line for that same folder in the same second. With this change the same harness reports 0 losses over 291,628 creates and 13,243 folder deletions.

The test added here is the deterministic form of that: it hooks the store listing to create an entry inside the window, then asserts the entry survives the folder delete. It fails on master and passes with the fix. It also pins what this change does *not* fix — the folder entry is still removed, so the surviving entry is reachable by path but absent from listings.

## Follow-up

That remaining exposure is handled in #10783, stacked on this branch: the cleaner records the folders it deleted each pass and restores any that turn out to hold entries. Closing it inside this function instead would need the emptiness check and the entry delete to be atomic, which is per-store — one statement on SQL, a Lua script on redis, but not expressible on leveldb2, where children hash by `md5(dir)` and the directory entry by `md5(parent)` into different partitions.

items.title: filer.remote.gateway: stop zero-byte uploads of remote-only entries
items.body: ## Summary Fixes #12109 — a 4.50 regression where `weed filer.remote.gateway` re-uploads every synced file as a **zero-byte object** after `remote.uncache` drops its local chunks, overwriting the good copy on the remote (and re-stamping the entry with the empty object's ETag, so S3 GET then fails). Root cause: since `shouldSendToRemote` started treating a cleared `LastLocalSyncTsNs` as dirty when the remote mtime shares the entry's second (the same-second rewrite fix), an uncache/eviction update reads as a content change needing upload. The mounted-directory sync (`filer.remote.sync`) gained the `isDroppedLocalCopy` guard, but the bucketed gateway processor's update path never did, so it called `retriedWriteFile` on the chunkless entry. - Same-entry updates of a dropped local copy are now skipped, mirroring `processUpdateEvent`. - Renames of remote-only entries no longer delete the source object and write an empty destination: the object is copied on the remote, the entry restamped (clearing the pending-source marker), and the source removed only while the stamp still describes it — the same protocol `completeRemoteOnlyRename` uses. A remote-only entry renamed out of coverage keeps its object, and the old-side delete only removes the object the event's stamp still describes. ## Test plan - [x] `TestGatewayDroppedLocalCopyIsNotUploaded` — the uncache update produces no write/delete/metadata update (fails before the fix: the chunkless entry is uploaded) - [x] `TestGatewayUncachedRewriteIsStillUploaded` — a rewrite of an uncached entry still uploads - [x] `TestGatewayRemoteOnlyRenameCopiesTheObject` / `TestGatewayRemoteOnlyRenameAlreadyComplete` — remote-only rename copies the source object / skips the copy when the destination already describes it, then removes the source - [x] `TestGatewayRenameOutKeepsRemoteOnlyObject` — rename out of coverage keeps the remote-only object - [x] `go test ./weed/command/` — all pass Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Prevented updates from replacing existing remote content with empty files when local copies have no content, while ensuring rewritten files with content are still uploaded. * Improved renames involving mounted storage buckets: remote-only content is copied when needed, already-copied content is retained, and sources are removed only when appropriate. * Preserved remote files when renaming items outside bucket coverage. * Avoided removing a source while another entry still depends on it.

items.title: filer: honor a storage rule's rack/data-center constraint instead of falling back
items.body: ## Summary Fixes https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/11803 `StorageOption.ToAssignRequests` has always emitted a second, location-stripped `altRequest` after the constrained one (added for grow-if-DC-full in an earlier change). When a rule names a rack or data center — e.g. a collection pinned to `rack=l1000` — the filer retries the constrained assign for the retry budget and then silently re-issues it *without* the constraint, so the write lands on any rack. The reporter sees `No writable volumes ... Rack:l1000` followed by volumes serving writes on a different rack. A location on a storage rule is a placement contract, not a preference: when nothing writable satisfies it, the assign must fail, never widen. "Prefer but allow elsewhere" is what an unset field already means. This removes the stripped fallback from `ToAssignRequests` and passes the single constrained request at its three call sites; `operation.Assign`'s variadic signature is unchanged for other callers. ## Changes - `operation`: `ToAssignRequests` returns the constrained request only; regression test asserts the location is carried. - filer write/remote/assign paths: call `operation.Assign` with the constrained request. #### Test plan - [x] `go test ./weed/operation/` - [ ] confirm an assign to a rule whose rack has no writable volumes fails instead of writing elsewhere Generated with [Devin](https://devin.ai) --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Storage assignments now respect explicitly specified data center, rack, or node locations without falling back to a different location. * Default locations can still fall back to an unrestricted placement when needed. * **Style** * Improved formatting of internal comments.

items.title: filer: cut ReaderCache mutex contention on small reads
items.body: ## Summary Fixes #11676 — the 4.47→4.48 regression where many concurrent small S3 GETs lost ~20% throughput while CPU usage dropped. Reproduced locally (`weed server -s3 -filer`, 4,096×4 KiB objects, 64 concurrent GETs, aws-sdk-go-v2, `-cpuprofile` for mutex/block profiles): | build | ops/s | mean | mutex delay (60 s) | |---|---|---|---| | 4.47 | 18,840 | 3.4 ms | 1,609 s | | 4.48 | 15,728 | 4.1 ms | **2,540 s** | | 4.48 + this PR | 20,397 | 3.1 ms | attribution below | The mutex profile pins it on `ReaderCache`'s global lock, which the pinning work in #11502/#11503 multiplied: each small read now took the cache-wide mutex for the downloader lookup, again in `unpin(previous)` → `removeConsumed`, again in `releaseIfFinished`, again in the read's deferred `removeConsumed`, and once more in `ReleaseStream`. With 64 streams the extra acquisitions form a convoy — goroutines park instead of running, which is exactly the reported "CPU down, latency up" signature. PUTs are unaffected; 1 MiB GETs hurt less because the fixed lock count amortizes over more bytes. ## Changes Keep the pinning correctness intact; reduce how often the shared lock is needed: - `removeConsumed` checks the consumable conditions (all atomics) before taking the lock, so per-read bookkeeping that cannot remove a cacher costs no lock acquisition. - `chunkStream` gets its own mutex for `cacher`: pin/detach lifecycle (`pin`, `releaseIfFinished`, `releaseStream`, `unpin`) no longer runs under the cache lock at all — the stream is only ever shared by concurrent `ReadAt` calls on one `ChunkReadAt`. - Downloader map lookups and read registration move to a read lock; only error eviction, insertion, and removal need the write lock. The `chunkCache` probe runs lock-free, and the insert path re-checks the map under the write lock. - `startCaching` goroutine spawn + `cacheStartedCh` handshake happen after releasing the write lock instead of inside it (both in `readChunkAt`'s insert path and `MaybeCache`). Destroy still runs after unlocking, registered reads still pin the buffer against `destroy()` (`wg.Add` under the map hold), and pin counters keep eviction preference — the shared-buffer lifetime guarantees from #11502/#11503 are unchanged. ## Test plan - [x] `go test -race ./weed/filer/` — all existing pin/eviction/shared-stream/cancellation tests pass - [x] New `TestReaderCacheBookkeepingOffCacheLock` — pin + releaseStream must complete while another goroutine holds the cache lock - [x] Benchmarked 4.48+fix vs 4.47 on identical data dir: throughput recovered and slightly exceeds 4.47 --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved reliability of cached file reads during concurrent access, including when a cache cannot serve a requested portion of a file. * Reduced contention during cache operations so concurrent reads and prefetching can proceed more smoothly. * Fixed cases where cache bookkeeping could block while a stream was being pinned or released, helping concurrent file access complete more reliably.

items.title: shell: clean up the target copy when a merge upload fails
items.body:
Reported in https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/11009#issuecomment-5508071217: "fs.mergeVolumes with volumes that are replicated creates a LOT of orphans".

That is right, for one specific reason. `topology.ReplicatedWrite` commits the needle to the local volume *before* it fans out to the other replicas, so an upload that reports failure can still have left a copy on the target. `moveChunk` returns the error, `fs.mergeVolumes` prints "failed to move" and carries on to the next chunk, and that copy stays behind forever: the filer is never re-pointed at it, so nothing will ever reference or delete it.

One sick replica orphans roughly half the chunks of a merge (two thirds with three copies): the entry node is picked at random by `LookupVolumeServerUrl`, and the replica upload uses `MaxAttempts: 1` ("fail fast on a dead replica; the client write retries") — except here there is no retrying client, so a single transient timeout per chunk is enough. A volume with a single copy has no such window: `GetWritableRemoteReplications` returns early, and the write is one local append that either succeeds or leaves nothing behind.

This deletes the needle we may have written, on every replica of the target, before continuing. The source side already did exactly this after a successful move, so `deleteMovedSourceNeedles` is renamed to `deleteOrphanedNeedles` and reused for both ends. The freshly assigned manifest needle in `uploadManifestChunk` has the same window and gets the same treatment.

## Verified on a 2-node cluster, replication 001

Merge with a healthy target: source needles deleted on both replicas, `volume.fsck` clean. Unchanged by this PR.

Merge into a target whose replica cannot accept the write (`volume.mark -node=... -readonly` on one copy):

before
```
dataNode:127.0.0.1:21002  volume:5  entries:11  orphan:3  27.27%  1572924B
Total                                entries:125  orphan:3   2.40%  1572924B
```
The target volume's replicas were left permanently divergent, 11 live needles vs 8.

after
```
Total                                entries:122  orphan:0   0.00%  0B
no orphan data
```
The stranded copies are written and then deleted (`FileCount 19 DeleteCount 10` vs `17/8`), so both replicas agree on 9 live needles and the dead bytes are reclaimable by vacuum. All 60 files read back byte-identical.

Note for anyone reproducing this: `volume.fsck`'s `-cutoffTimeAgo` defaults to 5 hours, so a run straight after a merge reports `orphan:0` either way. The runs above pass `-cutoffTimeAgo=1s`.

## Not addressed here

The same report asks for two other things. Marking the source read-only before draining it would not have fixed these orphans (they land on the *target*), and `createMergePlan` currently rejects a read-only source outright — `IsReadOnly()` is true for `readonlyCanDelete` too, so even `volume.mark -readonlyCanDelete` would not get past the plan. Having `fs.mergeVolumes` delete the drained volumes itself is a separate feature.

items.title: iam: optionally require an iam: grant for self-service access-key actions
items.body: # iam: optionally require an iam: grant for self-service access-key actions ## Summary `AuthorizeIamAction` lets every authenticated identity run `CreateAccessKey`, `DeleteAccessKey`, `UpdateAccessKey`, `ListAccessKeys` and `GetUser` on itself without any grant. #10593 kept this deliberately, and this PR leaves it as the default. It adds an opt-in for deployments that want AWS's behaviour, where these actions need an IAM policy like any other (the usual one grants them on `arn:aws:iam::*:user/${aws:username}`). ## Why Where identities hold data-plane rights only (a bucket policy or an `s3:` policy naming them), the implicit carve-out is the one IAM path such an identity has. If one of its keys leaks, the holder can mint further keys for the same identity, with no cap, and those keys keep working after the operator deletes the key that leaked. It can also deactivate or delete the keys the operator issued. An operator who rotates keys centrally has no way to switch this off today. ## What changed - New option, off by default: `-s3.iam.selfServiceRequiresGrant` on `weed server`, `weed filer` and `weed mini`, and `-iam.selfServiceRequiresGrant` on `weed s3` (`S3ApiServerOption.IamSelfServiceRequiresGrant`). - With it set, the five self-service actions need `iam:`. As with `CreateServiceAccount`'s scoping by policy resource, the grant is authorized against the target user's ARN, which is the caller's own when `UserName` is empty. A policy can therefore confine it to the caller's own keys (`arn:aws:iam:::user/${aws:username}` or a literal user ARN) or allow more. - The admin and `iam:*` grants are unaffected. With the option off nothing changes. ## Tests In `weed/s3api/s3api_embedded_iam_authz_test.go`: - `TestAuthorizeIamActionSelfServiceRequiresGrantWhenConfigured`: with the option set, an identity holding only `s3:*` and an identity with no policy are refused all five actions on an empty, own and other target. This test fails without the change. - `TestAuthorizeIamActionSelfServiceGrantIsScopedByResource`: a grant on `arn:aws:iam:::user/key_owner` or `arn:aws:iam:::user/${aws:username}` allows the five actions on the caller itself (implicit and explicit `UserName`) and refuses them on another user, and still refuses `CreateUser`. - `TestAuthorizeIamActionSelfServiceRequiresGrantKeepsAdmin`: the admin and an `iam:*` grant keep every action on every target. - `TestAuthorizeIamActionSelfServiceDefaultUnchanged`: option off, self-service allowed without a grant as before. `go test ./weed/s3api/ ./weed/iamapi/ ./weed/command/`: ok. `go vet` reports nothing in the touched files. ## Left out - The deprecated standalone `weed iam` server also accepts the option as `-selfServiceRequiresGrant` (its flags carry no `iam.` prefix). - Sibling actions that also act on the caller (for example `ListUserPolicies` and the service-account list, update and delete actions) are not part of the self-service carve-out and are unchanged. --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Added an option to require explicit IAM grants for self-service access-key management and user-record retrieval. - The setting is available through S3, Mini S3, and IAM command-line options and is disabled by default. - When enabled, grants are checked against the target user’s resource. Administrators and unrestricted IAM identities retain access, while anonymous identities remain denied. - **Documentation** - Added a description for the self-service IAM grant setting.

items.title: admin: stop the maintenance scanner pinning itself to one scan per second after a transient failure
items.body:
References #10874.

## What this actually fixes

The scan loop compared its target interval against the *configured* scan interval instead of the interval the ticker was actually running at. After a scan fails, the ticker shortens to a 1s error backoff. Once the failure clears, the comparison that's supposed to notice recovery and restore the normal cadence was structured so it never fired: a single transient scan error pinned the scanner to one scan per second for the rest of the process's life. That is almost certainly the multiplier behind #10874's ~658 KB/s log flood and 193k orphaned task-state files: `ScanWithTaskDetectors` cancels and re-saves the state of every pending task before each re-detection, so 172,800 scans over two days (matching a permanent 1s cadence) produces state-file counts in exactly that range, versus roughly 96 at the configured 30-minute cadence.

Alongside that, this also fixes:
- `GetTaskPolicy` dereferencing a nil `*MaintenancePolicy` and panicking the admin process. Reachable whenever `conf/maintenance.pb` is absent, which is the default state for `DefaultMaintenanceConfig()`.
- A `defer ticker.Stop()` bound to only the first ticker created (leaked on every backoff transition), and an unsynchronized `running` field read/written outside the manager's mutex.
- `LoadConfigFromPersistence(nil)` calls in `maintenance_manager.go` and a near-duplicate in `dash/config_persistence.go` that always failed their type assertion and silently fell back to hardcoded values instead of what was actually persisted (this was the original scope of #10874 as filed).
- Those hardcoded fallback values had drifted from each task's own `NewDefaultConfig()`: vacuum scan interval 2h vs the fallback's 24h, balance 30m/0.2 imbalance threshold vs 6h/0.1, erasure coding 1h/0.95 fullness/30MB min size vs 168h/0.90/1024MB. Now derived from one source instead of a second hand-maintained copy.
- `ec_balance` had no entry in the policy map and no `Load`/`SaveEcBalanceTaskPolicy` on `ConfigPersistence` at all, unlike the other three tasks.
- The maintenance manager's policy now reaches `GenericScheduler.GetMaxConcurrent`, so a persisted per-task concurrency limit is actually honored where before it wasn't consumed anywhere.

## What this does NOT fix

This does not fix "disabling a task in the admin UI doesn't work," which is the reporter's specific complaint. The admin UI writes a disable to `<dataDir>/plugin/job_types/volume_balance/config.pb` (the plugin config store). The legacy `MaintenanceManager`, which is what was looping, reads `<dataDir>/conf/task_balance.pb` (a separate store with a different name for the same task) — and that file has no HTTP writer anywhere in the codebase. The legacy manager is also started unconditionally, while `weed worker` only runs the plugin runtime, so nothing ever claims the tasks the legacy scanner keeps detecting under its compiled-in `Enabled: true`.

I'd rather flag that than paper over it. Unifying the two stores, or retiring the legacy scanner now that the plugin runtime exists, is a real design decision I don't think a PR should make unilaterally. Happy to take either direction if you'd like, or to leave it as a separate issue.

## Testing

New regression test for the ticker (`TestScanLoopRestoresIntervalAfterBackoff`): seeds a failed scan, lets the loop drop into the 1s backoff, lets the next scan succeed, and asserts the loop returns to the configured cadence rather than staying at 1s. Reverting just the comparison this PR changes makes it fail with 4-5 scans in a 5s window against a 3s configured interval, matching the reported symptom's shape. Plus tests for the nil-policy guard, the policy reaching `GenericScheduler`/`GenericDetector`, `ec_balance`'s policy round-trip, and the corrected defaults matching `NewDefaultConfig()`.

`go build ./weed/admin/... ./weed/worker/...`, `go vet`, and `go test -race ./weed/admin/... ./weed/worker/...` are all clean.

items.title: filer: apply the path's storage rule TTL on every write path
items.body:
Fixes #10962.

### The reported path is already fixed

`ObjectTransaction` -> `applyObjectMutation` -> `Filer::CreateEntry` did skip the storage-rule TTL that `FilerServer::CreateEntry` applies. That was fixed in #10196, which pulled the stamping into `applyStorageDefaultsToEntry` and called it from both handlers; the fix is in 4.38 and later, so upgrading from the reported 4.34 resolves it.

Reverting that one call reproduces the report exactly - an object written through `ObjectTransaction` under a 3 minute `fs.configure` TTL lands with `ttlSec 0`:

```
--- FAIL: TestObjectTransactionPutAppliesRuleTtl
    entry TtlSec = 0, want 180
```

The first commit adds that as a regression test so the two write paths cannot drift apart again.

### Three sibling paths still drop the TTL

Chasing the same rule through the rest of the filer turned up three write paths that resolve the storage option from the path - so their chunks *do* go to a TTL volume - but never stamp the TTL on the entry they store. The entry then outlives the data it points at:

- `AppendToEntry`: a new entry is created with `ttlSec 0` while its chunks are assigned under the rule.
- TUS completion: `tusWriteData` uploads under the target path's rule, then `completeTusUpload` builds the final entry with `ttlSec 0`.
- The copy handler: chunks are re-uploaded under the destination's option, but the entry keeps the *source's* `ttlSec`, which is 0 for a source outside the prefix.

Each is one commit, routed through the existing `applyStorageDefaultsToEntry` rather than a new helper. The helper now feeds the entry's own TTL into `detectStorageOption` instead of a hardcoded 0, so an existing entry's TTL still drives where its appended chunks land. TUS completion also drops its hand-rolled read-only check (`applyStorageDefaultsToEntry` already returns `ErrReadOnly`) and picks up the rule's name-length limit.

### Tests

`TestCopyAppliesRuleTtl` and `TestCompleteTusUploadAppliesRuleTtl` both fail on master and pass here. `AppendToEntry` takes a cluster lock on entry, so it has no unit test in this package; the change there is the same three-line swap.

The whole `weed/server` package is green.

No Rust mirror: the Rust side is a volume server, and none of this lives outside the Go filer.

items.title: Maintenance system cannot be disabled: admin_server.go force-enables it at startup, and the legacy /maintenance UI routes are gone
items.body:
## Summary

`MaintenanceConfig.Enabled` is documented as "Toggle this to enable or disable the entire maintenance system", but it cannot be set to `false` in practice. `weed/admin/dash/admin_server.go` unconditionally flips it back to `true` at startup, immediately before the value is used to decide whether to start the manager.

Combined with the removal of the legacy `/maintenance` UI routes, the legacy `MaintenanceManager` is effectively always-on and unconfigurable.

Verified present on `master` (`34bb444f33d5`) and on tags 4.37 through 4.43.

## Root cause

`weed/admin/dash/admin_server.go` (lines 268–273 on master):

```go
// Force enable maintenance system for new default behavior
// This handles the case where old configs had Enabled=false as default
if !maintenanceConfig.Enabled {
	glog.V(1).Infof("Enabling maintenance system (new default behavior)")
	maintenanceConfig.Enabled = true
}

glog.V(1).Infof("Maintenance system initialized with persistent configuration (enabled: %v)", maintenanceConfig.Enabled)
```

...and about ten lines later, the value that was just overwritten is the sole gate on starting the manager:

```go
// Start maintenance manager if enabled
if maintenanceConfig.Enabled {
	go func() {
		time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)
		if err := server.StartMaintenanceManager(); err != nil {
```

So the persisted setting is loaded, schema defaults are applied over it, and then any `false` is discarded. There is no code path in which a user-set `Enabled: false` survives to the `if` that consumes it.

The intent in the comment is clear — migrate old configs whose default was `false` — but as written it does not distinguish "defaulted to false in an old schema" from "explicitly set to false by the operator", so it permanently overrides the latter.

## The toggle also has no UI

The schema still advertises the field (`weed/admin/maintenance/config_schema.go`):

```go
{
	Name:         "enabled",
	JSONName:     "enabled",
	Type:         config.FieldTypeBool,
	DefaultValue: true,
	DisplayName:  "Enable Maintenance System",
	Description:  "When enabled, the system will automatically scan for and execute maintenance tasks",
	HelpText:     "Toggle this to enable or disable the entire maintenance system",
	InputType:    "checkbox",
```

But on a running 4.37 admin server, the routes that would expose it are gone:

```
/maintenance                     -> 404
/maintenance/config              -> 404
/api/admin/maintenance/config    -> 404
```

Consistent with that, no `maintenance.pb` / `maintenance.json` is ever written under `<dataDir>/conf` — the config cannot be persisted because nothing can write it. `SaveMaintenanceConfig` exists in `config_persistence.go` but appears to have no remaining caller reachable from the UI.

The net result is a scheduler that runs unconditionally, has no configuration surface, and is invisible to the operator — while the plugin scheduler (which *does* have a UI and honours `enabled` correctly at `weed/admin/plugin/plugin_scheduler.go:464`) runs alongside it against a separate config store.

## Why this matters

This is the reason the defect in #10874 is not recoverable by configuration. There, the legacy detector re-enables a disabled `volume_balance` task from compiled-in defaults; here, the operator has no way to switch off the subsystem that is running it. Together they produced a detect/cancel loop that ran for ~2 days at ~658 KB/s of log output and left 193,705 orphaned task files, with no supported way to stop it short of patching or blocking it externally.

The two issues are independent defects, but either one alone would have been recoverable.

## Suggested fix

Whichever of these matches the intended direction:

1. **Scope the migration.** Only force-enable when the loaded config is genuinely absent or pre-schema, rather than on every `false`. A "config version" or a distinct "never explicitly set" sentinel would separate the two cases the current code conflates.
2. **Drop the override.** If maintenance-on is now simply the default, the schema `DefaultValue: true` plus `ApplyDefaultsToProtobuf` already achieves that for new configs, without overriding explicit operator intent.
3. **Restore or replace the config surface.** If the legacy manager is meant to stay, it needs a way to configure it; if it is meant to be superseded by the plugin scheduler, it probably should not be starting unconditionally in parallel with it.

Happy to test a patch against our cluster if that would help.

## Environment

- SeaweedFS 4.37 (also verified in source on 4.38–4.43 and `master` @ `34bb444f33d5`)
- `weed admin` with `-dataDir` set, running in Docker
- 3 masters, 8 volume servers
- Related: #10874 (legacy manager ignores persisted task configs)

items.title: filer: restore a folder that received an entry while it was deleted
items.body:
Follows #10782, now merged, and rebased onto it.

#10782 stopped the empty-folder cleaner from destroying an object that arrives between the emptiness check and the delete. What it left behind is the milder half of the same race: the entry survives, but the directory holding it does not.

The cleaner checks that a folder is empty and then deletes it, and those two steps are not atomic. An entry created in between ends up reachable by its own path — `FindEntry` keys on the full path and never consults the parent — but absent from `ListObjectsV2` and every other traversal, because the directory that would have carried it is gone. It stays that way until some later write into the same folder happens to recreate the parent.

That is why this is a follow-up rather than part of the fix: a HEAD still succeeds, so read-after-write verification never sees it. It shows up as an object missing from a listing, and for disk layouts that derive their state from listing the bucket rather than from local metadata, as data that has effectively vanished.

## The metadata stream already knows

A folder is recorded before it is deleted. For an entry to be orphaned it has to be created after the emptiness check inside the delete, which is after that record — so its create event always arrives while the folder is still being watched, and that event names the exact directory.

So the cleaner does not go looking. `OnCreateEvent` matches the directory against the recently deleted folders, and a hit means that folder is known to need putting back. No polling, no listing per folder per pass, and no guessing when the racing write will land.

The folder is then restored with the mode, uid, gid and user/group names read from it *before* it was deleted, so a restore cannot hand back a directory that grants access the original denied. Missing ancestors are restored too, shallowest first, since the eager parent cascade may have taken them in the same pass. One listing is done before restoring, to skip the work when the entry has since gone away again.

The observation window is no longer a guess at the race. It bounds how far behind the event stream may run before a folder stops being watched — relevant because a write on a peer filer reaches this one through the aggregator.

Remaining limits, stated rather than implied: the watched set is in memory, so a filer restart between the delete and the restore leaves the orphan until a later write recreates the parent, and the set is bounded, with anything past the bound logged rather than dropped silently. In both cases the entry itself is never lost, only its place in listings.

## The redis stores need the opposite fix

On leveldb and the SQL stores a child records its own directory, so a listing is derived and the orphan is recoverable. On redis it is not: `ListDirectoryEntries` is nothing but a read of `genDirectoryListKey(dir)`, and `DeleteEntry` opened by deleting that key outright.

So the racing entry lost its membership immediately, and no repair could reach it. The listing is now dropped in `DeleteFolderChildren`, alongside the children it describes, and left alone in `DeleteEntry`. The plain redis store was leaking the key altogether. redis3 needed two changes: `removeChildren` clears the skip list nodes but not the list itself, and `removeChild` was writing an empty list back rather than deleting it, so an emptied directory left a header that nothing would collect once the sweep was skipped.

## Tests

`TestEmptyFolderCleaner_restoreFoldersWrittenDuringDelete` covers the event path: a create event for the deleted folder puts it back, one for a different folder is ignored, an entry that went away again is not restored, observation expires, a failed restore is retried, and a delete that reports failure is still observed.

`TestEnsureDirectoryEntryRestoresRacingParent` drives the real thing over leveldb2 — it creates an entry inside the delete window, asserts the folder has dropped out of its parent's listing, then asserts the restore brings it back. `TestEnsureDirectoryEntryRestoresExactAttributes` asserts a `0700` directory returns as `0700` with its owner intact.

`TestDeleteEntryKeepsChildListing` (redis2, redis3), `TestDeleteFolderChildrenRemovesTheListing` (redis) and `TestRemovingTheLastChildDropsTheListing` (redis3) cover the store changes. They run against a live redis under `RUN_REDIS_TESTS=1`; verified against redis 7 both ways.
